## Part VI — Cross-cutting (F61 … F64)

### 6.0 What this part specifies, and what it deliberately does not

Parts III to V specify what the platform reads and the surfaces it renders. This part specifies four capabilities that sit **underneath** all of them, and that is why it is shaped differently.

| Feature | What this part fixes | What it does not |
|---|---|---|
| **F61** | The notification and correspondence **engine** — template model, channel routing, queueing, retry, bounce handling, idempotency | The **content**. Every message, its wording, its parameters and its channel are A2's, and no sentence from A2 is restated here |
| **F62** | The access-control **mechanism** — how a permission and a data scope are represented, resolved and enforced | The **matrix**. Who may do what, on whose data, is A3's, and no row of it is restated here |
| **F63** | The audit log's **schema, coverage and constraints** | The business rules it serves — D1 §7.5 `BR-AUDIT-1…5` |
| **F64** | The non-functional **baseline the platform is built to**, and what degraded operation looks like | The business-level targets — D1 §8 `NFR-1…10` |

**Three conventions apply to this part specifically.**

1. **These are record tables, not screen tables.** §2.2's columns are kept, because a developer reading a table in this document should not have to learn a second format — but *Source* is `system` on any field the platform writes and never a person, and *On error* is `—` on those rows rather than an A2 code, because a field nobody types has no validation message. **§2.2 now carries this exception explicitly** — a record table whose fields are system-written may leave *On error* empty — so this part cites it rather than declaring a deviation of its own. §2.2 also restricts the exception to Part VI: no screen section anywhere else may use it.
2. **The administration screens for these records live in Part V, under F55** (users, roles, thresholds, master data) and A3 §3.1. Part VI defines *what the record holds and what the engine does with it*; Part V defines *the screen an administrator sees*. Message codes for the field-level validation of those screens are allocated in Part V and consolidated in Part VIII.
3. **Validation identifiers in the `V-6nn` range are reserved for Part VI** and are consolidated in Part VIII with the rest.

**A code marked †** in any table below **does not exist in A2 v1.0** and is requested by this part. §6.5 lists all of them in one place. Per §2.2, this document may not write the wording — only ask for the code.

---

### 6.1 Notification and correspondence engine (F61)

**Purpose.** One engine renders and delivers every message in A2, on every channel, to every actor — and never lets a delivery failure become a claim outcome.

**Entered from** — no screen. The engine is invoked by domain events, never by a user action.
**Who may configure it** — `ADMIN`, scope `MASTER` (A3 §3.1, F61 row). Nobody else, including an approver, may edit a template.

#### 6.1.1 The division of ownership, stated once

A2 owns the message: its code, its wording in both languages, its named parameters, its channel(s), and the rules M-1…M-10 that constrain all four. F61 owns the machinery: template storage, parameter binding, rendering, channel dispatch, retry, and the operator queue when dispatch fails.

**The practical consequence for a developer.** A new message is a row in A2 plus a template record here. A change of wording is a change to A2 that propagates into a new template *version*; it is never a code change. If a behaviour cannot be expressed without editing A2, the correct action is to raise the A2 change (A2 §11), not to build around it.

#### 6.1.2 Channels

**A2 §0.3 defines six channel tokens, and the sixth is new at A2 v1.1.** The engine implements them as follows.

| Channel | Implemented as | Recipient | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `IN_APP` | A notification record on the customer's account, rendered in the app's notification list and, where the message concerns a claim, on that claim's timeline (F28) | `CUST` | **The in-app record is the record** for a customer. Every customer message that goes anywhere else also goes here — so a failed email or a suppressed push never costs the customer the information |
| `PUSH` | A device notification through the mobile push service, to the devices registered against the account (F21) | `CUST` | Carries only the push text A2 gives it. Never the in-app text. Never an amount, diagnosis, benefit name or decline reason — `BR-MSG-1`, A2 §0.3 |
| `EMAIL` | An email to **the recipient list of §6.1.2a** for a customer message, or to **the resolved staff recipient of §6.1.2b** for a staff message, with the generated PDF attached where the message is a `LETTER` | `CUST`, **and a named `ASSESSOR`, `APPROVER` or `ADMIN`** | The only channel that carries a document. **From A2 v1.1 it addresses either recipient group** — *"the constraint was always the recipient group, never the channel"* (A2 §0.3). **Which group a given message belongs to is A2's, per message** |
| **`STAFF_INBOX`** | **A notification record addressed to one named console user**, read from the bell on the console shell and surfaced at **§5.23**. **A real delivery channel**: queued in the outbox, rendered from a versioned template, retried, stored, and carrying a read/unread state | **A named `ASSESSOR`, `APPROVER` or `ADMIN` — never a role and never a queue** | **New at A2 v1.1.** It is the staff-side counterpart of `IN_APP` and is a separate token because the two differ in every property that matters to the engine: the addressee is a user rather than an account, the record is read on the console rather than in the app, and it carries a read state that `IN_APP` does not |
| `CONSOLE` | A message surfaced synchronously in the web console at the point of the action that raised it | `ASSESSOR`, `APPROVER`, `ADMIN` | **Not a delivery channel.** It is not queued, not retried and not stored in the outbox; it is the response to a request. **The test A2 §0.2 gives is one question — is there a person waiting for this response?** If yes it is `CONSOLE`; if the event happened whether or not anyone was watching it is `STAFF_INBOX`, and the engine treats the two as different in kind rather than as two renderings of one thing |
| `SMS` | An adapter interface with no configured provider and no route | — | No message in A2 uses it (A2 §9). See §6.1.9 |

**Channel is a property of the message, not of the engine or the recipient.** A2 rule M-9 states it, and the engine reads it from the template record rather than deciding it. There is no per-customer channel preference in MVP 1 (§6.1.9) — every message A2 defines is transactional, and an opt-out from a transactional message is a decision the business has not taken. **There is no per-staff preference either, and for a stronger reason**: a member of staff who could mute the bell could mute a claim's overdue alert, which is the one alert the console has no other way of raising.

> **`STAFF_INBOX` is carried here and its content is not. `A2 §8.1` owns the family and D2 yields to it** (§0.5). A2 §8.1 defines the eight `STAFF-NOTIF` messages, their triggers, their recipients, their Vietnamese and English wording, which two of the eight also go by `EMAIL`, and the seven rules **S-1 to S-7** they obey — including **S-3**, that a `STAFF_INBOX` notification carries no clinical detail, and **S-4**, that `EMAIL` is used on exactly two of the eight. **None of that is restated here**, on the same rule §6.0 applies to every other message in the catalogue: this part specifies the engine and never the content. **What Part VI owes is §6.1.2b — how a staff recipient is resolved, how the inbox is read, and what happens when the addressee is gone.**

> **This is `D2-127` closed, and it is closed by yielding rather than by arguing.** This table carried no staff recipient group until this pass and §6.1.9 excluded staff email outright; **A2 v1.1 §8.1 has since specified the family, the channel and the rules, and A2 owns message content, channel and wording** (§0.5). A2 §10 records the same contradiction from its side as **A2-06**. **§6.1.9 carries the full note and what the exclusion cost while it stood.**

> **One discrepancy, resolved in favour of A2.** Framework §7.1's one-line feature statement for F61 reads *"in-app, email, templated, bilingual catalogue"* and does not name push. A2 routes eleven messages to `PUSH` and D1 `BR-MSG-1` legislates its content. The Framework line is a summary written before A2 existed; A2 and D1 are the later and more specific statements, and §0.5 makes A2 the owner of a message's definition. **Push is in scope.** Recorded as open item **D2-81** so the Framework line is corrected rather than left to be discovered as a scope argument during build.

#### 6.1.2a The recipient list — who an email actually goes to

*(Register: **B-09**)*

**v0.2 said an email goes to "the address on the member record", and the member record has no address.** That is `G-B-03`: `insured_member` (§3.2.7) carries no email column, so the `EMAIL` channel as specified delivered to a field that does not exist. Every message A2 routes to email has been, on paper, undeliverable.

**A customer-facing email is addressed to the list below, in this order, and it is a list rather than a field because the person insured and the person asking are not always the same person.**

| # | Recipient | Presence | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **The claimant's email** — `claimant.email`, §3.2.10 | **Always.** Mandatory on the record | It is the only address in the model we capture ourselves, from the person who asked, at the moment they asked. On a claim where the claimant is the insured it is the insured's address; on a claim where they are not, it is the address of the person who will read the reply and act on it |
| 2 | **The insured member's email**, where InsureMO returns one | **Where present** | Additional, never instead. A guardian's claim for a minor should not be the only route by which the household learns the outcome — but a minor has no email and an employee on a group policy may have given their employer's, so it cannot be the primary |
| 3 | **A configured business mailbox, in copy** | **Where configured.** `config`, off by default | The reference copies a shared operational mailbox on every customer letter. It is useful and it is a **decision with a data-protection consequence**, so it is a switch an administrator sets rather than a behaviour the engine has. **It carries the same content as the customer's copy, including the settlement amount and the benefit table** |

**Three rules on the list.**

| # | Rule |
|---|---|
| **F61-R11** | **The list is resolved at the moment of dispatch, from the claim, and stored on the outbox row.** A resend goes to the addresses the original went to — the same argument as F61-R8 for the letter's bytes and template versioning for its words. An email resent to a changed address is a second, different notification wearing the first one's identity. **§5.22.1 already records the address a message went to and §5.22's V-719 re-sends to it**; this is the engine's half of the same rule |
| **F61-R12** | **An empty list is a failure, not a silent success.** Where recipient 1 is somehow absent — which V-404 should make impossible — the outbox row is marked `FAILED` with the reason, and it reaches the operator queue (§6.1.6). It is never marked sent |
| **F61-R13** | **The list is per message, not per claim.** A message whose A2 definition names a narrower audience uses the narrower one. Nothing here overrides A2 |

> **The reference also copies the issuing organisational unit's mailbox, and we do not**, because we do not model the concept (§3.3.1's `orgUnit` is a pass-through, not an entity). If InsureMO returns one and the business wants it copied, it is a fourth row on the list and nothing else changes.

> **What is deliberately unchanged.** `IN_APP` remains the record — every message that goes anywhere else also goes there (§6.1.2) — and this section changes only who receives the copy that leaves the building. **A failed email still costs the customer nothing**, because the in-app record already carried it.

> **`D2-14` is what recipient 2 waits on.** Whether InsureMO's member register holds an email address is still InsureMO's to answer; recipient 1 is what makes correspondence work either way. **This section is the customer list and only the customer list** — a staff recipient is resolved by §6.1.2b, from the console user record, and never from this list. **The two never mix**: A2 §0.4's recipient groups obey different content rules, and a resolver that could return an address from either group is how a message written for one group reaches the other.

#### 6.1.2b The staff recipient — how one is resolved, and what happens when they are gone

**A2 §8.1 owns the `STAFF` family and this section owns none of it.** What follows is the engine's half: given a message A2 addresses to a member of staff, **who is the address, where is the record read, and what does the engine do when the person is no longer there.** The eight messages, their triggers, their wording and which two also go by `EMAIL` are A2 §8.1's and are not restated.

**Resolution — one message, one named user.**

| # | Rule |
|---|---|
| **F61-R14** | **A staff recipient is a `user_id`, resolved at the moment of dispatch, and stored on the outbox row.** It is never a role, never a queue and never a distribution list. The resolution is performed by the domain event that raised the message — the assignee of the claim, the assessor who submitted the plan, the approver who returned it — because the event knows which person the fact is about and the engine does not |
| **F61-R15** | **A trigger that names more than one recipient produces more than one message**, one outbox row and one inbox record per user, each with its own delivery outcome and its own read state. A2's reassignment notice addresses three people; that is three rows. **A single row with three addressees would give three people one read state**, and the first to open it would mark it read for the other two |
| **F61-R16** | **The address for `EMAIL` on a staff message is the user record's email** (§6.2.6), never a claim-derived address and never §6.1.2a's list. `V-611` already makes it well-formed and unique. **The sender identity is `config`** and is A2 open item **A2-08** — §7's customer-facing sender and an internal one are not necessarily the same, and neither is template text |
| **F61-R17** | **Resolution failure is a failure, not a silent success** — the same rule as F61-R12 for the customer list. A staff message whose recipient cannot be resolved is marked `FAILED` on the outbox with the reason and reaches the operator queue (§6.1.6). It is never dropped and never re-pointed at a supervisor |

**Reading the inbox, and marking it read.**

| # | Rule |
|---|---|
| **F61-R18** | **The inbox record is written by the dispatcher and read by exactly one user** — the addressee. Scope is applied at the query and again at the link (§5.23.3 V-721c). **No role reads another user's inbox and there is no digest to a supervisor** (A2 §8.1 S-5, A3 §5) |
| **F61-R19** | **Read state is per record and is set by opening it** (§5.23.2 F6). It is **never set by the bell being opened**, never cleared by age, and never set by the engine. A count that clears itself is a count nobody trusts |
| **F61-R20** | **A notification is never deleted** (V-721d). Read and unread are the only two states, and every one of the eight also writes a row in the claim's correspondence history (§5.22, V-718; A2 §8.1 S-6) — **delivered or failed**, because the history answers *what did we send about this claim* and a staff message missing from it makes that answer quietly incomplete |
| **F61-R21** | **`STAFF_INBOX` is not re-sendable to an external address.** §5.22's manual re-send (V-719) refuses a staff-facing message, and A2 §8.2's `CLM-CONSOLE-017` is the refusal. The engine enforces it on the outbox row's recipient group, not on the screen |

**When the recipient has left, or is not there to read it.**

| Situation | What the engine does |
|---|---|
| **The user is `SUSPENDED` or `DISABLED` at dispatch** (§6.2.6 U8) | **The record is still written and the outbox row is still marked delivered.** It is **not** sent by `EMAIL`, and the row carries the reason. **The work has not gone away because the person has** — and the operator queue is told, so that the claim is reassigned by a person rather than rediscovered by the ageing report |
| **The user is deleted** | **There is no such state.** §6.2.6 U8: *a user is never deleted* — the audit trail references them forever, and the same property is what keeps an addressee resolvable. A notification addressed to a user who no longer exists is not a case this engine has to handle, and that is a property of the user model rather than of this section |
| **The user has no active session — they are simply not logged in** | **Nothing.** `STAFF_INBOX` is asynchronous by construction: A2 §0.2's test is *is there a person waiting for this response*, and the answer for every `STAFF-NOTIF` is no. The record waits on the bell and is read at the next sign-in. **This is the one property that distinguishes it from `CONSOLE`**, which has no meaning without a session and is therefore never queued |
| **The user is not at the console at all, for days** | **The two messages A2 §8.1 sends by `EMAIL` are the answer** — the returned claim and the overdue claim — and the reason only two do is A2's rule **S-4**, not this engine's. The other six wait |
| **The notification store is unavailable** | The bell shows an outage marker and **the console stays fully usable** (§5.23.4). A notification channel that can block work has become a dependency, which is what §6.1.6 forbids for the customer and forbids here for the same reason |

#### 6.1.3 The template model

A rendered message is produced from exactly four things, and nothing else:

```
template( messageCode, channel, language, version )   →   body with {namedParameters}
+ parameter set supplied by the triggering event
+ formatting rules (money, date, datetime — §2.3 and A2 M-4)
=  a complete rendered body
```

**Four rules, and the first is the one that matters.**

| # | Rule |
|---|---|
| **F61-R1** | **A sentence is never assembled from fragments.** Every message is a single complete template with named parameters substituted into it. The engine has no concatenation primitive, no "reason phrase" table appended to a stem, and no conditional clause spliced in at runtime. This is §2.6, and it exists because Vietnamese classifiers and word order do not survive fragment assembly — a stem plus a fragment produces a sentence that is grammatical in English and wrong in Vietnamese. *(§2.6 rests this on A2 rule **M-8**, which reads "placeholders are named, never positional" — a rule the no-fragment-assembly rule depends on but is not identical to, and the nearest alternative, M-2, is "every message says what to do next". **No rule in A2 v1.0 states the prohibition literally**; the engine is built to it regardless. Open item **D2-89** — A2 to state it as a rule of its own rather than leave it inferred.)* |
| **F61-R2** | **Placeholders are named, never positional** (A2 M-8). `{benefitName}`, never `{0}`. The engine rejects a positional placeholder at template save, not at render |
| **F61-R3** | **The template holds no formatting.** `{settlementAmount}` renders as `1.200.000 đ` because the renderer applies §2.3's `money` rules and A2 M-4, not because the template says so. A template that carried its own separator would drift from the rest of the system the first time one of them changed |
| **F61-R4** | **A parameter the event does not supply is an error, not an empty string.** Rendering halts, the outbox row is marked `FAILED` with the missing parameter named, and it goes to the operator queue (§6.1.6). A settlement notice that reads *"Số tiền chi trả: "* is worse than one that was never sent |

**Where the same code renders two different sentences.** A2 gives several messages a distinct push text — `CLM-NOTIF-005` carries the amount in-app and by email and says only that a result exists on the lock screen. That is **two template records under one message code**, differing in `channel`. It is not a conditional inside one template, and F61-R1 is why.

**Language.** Template records exist in `VI` and `EN` (A2 M-1). The engine's selection rule is not a user preference: **a recipient on `IN_APP`, `PUSH` or `EMAIL` always receives `VI`**; `EN` exists for the console, for testing and for the team. There is no code path that can send `EN` to a customer.

#### 6.1.4 Field table — notification template record

| # | Label (VI) | Type | Source | Req | Validation | On error |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T1 | Mã thông điệp | `text(20)` | `master` | M | `V-601` — must be a code that exists in A2; format `<AREA>-<TYPE>-<NNN>` per A2 §0.2 | *(new A2 item needed — **D2-88**)* |
| T2 | Kênh | `enum(Channel)` | `master` | M | `V-602` — must be a channel A2 lists against this code | *(new A2 item needed — **D2-88**)* |
| T3 | Ngôn ngữ | `enum(Language)` | `master` | M | `VI` or `EN` | *(new A2 item needed — **D2-88**)* |
| T4 | Phiên bản | `int` | `system` | M | Allocated on save; never edited | — |
| T5 | Tiêu đề | `text(150)` | `user` | C | Mandatory where T2 = `EMAIL`; must be empty otherwise. `V-603` | *(new A2 item needed — **D2-88**)* |
| T6 | Nội dung | `textarea(4000)` | `user` | M | `V-604` — every `{placeholder}` must be named (F61-R2) and must be in the parameter set the trigger supplies; an unknown placeholder is rejected at save | *(new A2 item needed — **D2-88**)* |
| T7 | Tham số | `derived` | `system` | — | Parsed from T6 at save. Stored so a change to the trigger that drops a parameter fails loudly against every template that used it | — |
| T8 | Tệp đính kèm | `enum(AttachmentType)` | `master` | C | Mandatory where the A2 `TYPE` segment is `LETTER`; must be empty otherwise | *(new A2 item needed — **D2-88**)* |
| T9 | Hiệu lực từ | `datetime` | `user` | M | Not in the past on save | *(new A2 item needed — **D2-88**)* |
| T10 | Trạng thái | `enum(TemplateStatus)` | `system` | M | `DRAFT` → `ACTIVE` → `SUPERSEDED`. Exactly one `ACTIVE` per (T1, T2, T3) at any instant | — |
| T11 | Người cập nhật | `lookup(User)` | `system` | M | Written on save; audited (§6.3) | — |
| T12 | Thời điểm cập nhật | `datetime` | `system` | M | | — |

**Templates are versioned and never edited in place.** A saved change supersedes the previous version; the previous version is retained. This is not tidiness: §6.1.6's manual resend re-renders from **the version recorded on the outbox row**, so a customer who receives the same notice twice receives the same words twice. A resend that picked up newer wording would produce two different settlement notices for one settlement.

#### 6.1.5 Delivery — queue, retry, bounce

**The outbox.** A notification is written as an outbox row **in the same database transaction as the event that caused it**. Not after it, not from a listener that might not run.

> **Why this is non-negotiable.** The two failures either side of it are both silent and both serious. Write the notification before the transaction commits and a customer can be told a claim was approved that then rolled back. Write it after and an approval that succeeds can leave no one told — and the claim looks, to the customer, exactly like one that is stuck. The outbox row and the state transition succeed or fail together.

A dispatcher then reads the outbox, renders, calls the channel adapter, and records the attempt. The dispatcher is a separate process from the transaction that wrote the row, which is what makes a slow mail server unable to slow down an approval.

**Retry.** D3 §1.3 sets the platform's retry policy for interface calls: exponential backoff 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, 16s — five retries, six attempts — then stop and raise an operational alert. That schedule is correct for a synchronous call with a human waiting on the answer. **It is wrong for email**, where the common transient failure is a receiving mail server deferring for minutes.

| Channel | Retry schedule | Status |
|---|---|---|
| `IN_APP` | None. The write is local and either succeeds or is a database failure | — |
| **`STAFF_INBOX`** | **None, for the same reason as `IN_APP`** — the write is local. **A failed write is not retried and is not swallowed**: the outbox row is marked `FAILED` and reaches the operator queue, because the alternative is a member of staff who is never told and never knows they were not told | — |
| `PUSH` | D3 §1.3 as written — 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, 16s, then stop | Cited |
| `EMAIL` | 1 min, 5 min, 15 min, 1 hour, 4 hours — five retries, six attempts, then stop and raise. **The schedule is the channel's and is the same for both recipient groups** — an internal mail server greylists exactly as an external one does | **Proposed** — D3 §1.3's schedule exhausts in 31 seconds, which abandons every message that hit a two-minute greylist |
| `CONSOLE` | Not applicable — synchronous | — |

The `4xx`/`5xx` distinction from D3 §1.3 holds: a provider `4xx` other than `429` is not retried, because a malformed recipient address does not become well-formed on the second attempt.

**Bounces.**

| Event | What the engine does |
|---|---|
| **Soft bounce** (mailbox full, greylisted, temporary deferral) | Treated as a retryable failure and re-queued on the schedule above |
| **Hard bounce** (address does not exist, domain does not resolve, permanently rejected) | The address is marked `UNDELIVERABLE` — **on the claimant record for a customer message, on the user record (§6.2.6) for a staff one**. **No further email is attempted to it** until an administrator clears the flag. An operator queue entry is raised (*(new A2 item needed — **D2-88**)*) |
| **Any bounce** | **The in-record copy of the same message is unaffected**: `IN_APP` remains the customer's record of it, and `STAFF_INBOX` remains the officer's. **A bounce is never re-routed to another channel** — pushing a settlement amount to a lock screen because an email failed would breach `BR-MSG-1` to solve an unrelated problem, and re-routing a staff message to a customer channel would breach A2 §0.4's group rules to solve the same one |

**Ordering.** Outbox rows for one claim dispatch in the order the events occurred. An information request that arrived after an approval notice would read as though the claim had reopened.

**Reminders.** `DOC-NOTIF-005` is a scheduled reminder, dispatched by `SYSTEM` against claims in `PENDING_INFO`. Fires on **day 3 and day 7** after `requestedAt`, then stops. **Both figures proposed** — no source in this document set sets a reminder cadence.

#### 6.1.6 When a notification fails — and why that is never a claim outcome

This is the point of A2 rule M-6 and §2.10 applied to F61 specifically, so it is stated as rules rather than prose.

| # | Rule |
|---|---|
| **F61-R5** | **A notification failure changes no claim state.** There is no transition, in Part VII's matrix or anywhere else, whose trigger is a delivery failure. A claim that was `APPROVED` when the email bounced is still `APPROVED` |
| **F61-R6** | **A notification failure is never visible to the customer.** It does not appear on the claim timeline, it produces no in-app message, and it is not counted in the claim's status. The failure is an operational fact about our infrastructure, and the customer's claim is unaffected by it |
| **F61-R7** | **A failure surfaces to an operator, in a queue, with everything needed to act.** Never as a log line somebody might read |
| **F61-R7a** | **All three rules hold for a staff message and one of them holds more sharply.** A2 §8.1's rule **S-2** is F61-R5 stated from the catalogue's side, and `V-721a` is the same rule on the screen. **F61-R7 is the one that matters more here**: a customer whose message failed still has the `IN_APP` record, so nothing is lost; **a staff message that failed to write has no second copy anywhere**, and the person it was for cannot miss what they were never shown. The queue is the only place that failure exists |

**The operator queue.** A console view, `ADMIN` only, scope `MASTER` (A3 §3.1 — F61 is an administration function; it carries no claim data beyond the reference).

| Column | Content |
|---|---|
| Message | `messageCode`, channel, template version |
| Claim / policy | `claimNo` or `policyNo` — **a reference only.** No amount, no diagnosis, no benefit name. An administrator has no grant over clinical detail (A3 §4.11) and a failure queue is not a way around it |
| Recipient | Masked — last four of a phone number, local part elided on an email address. **A staff recipient is shown as the login name, unmasked**, because an administrator already administers the user record (A3 §3.1) and a masked colleague is a row nobody can act on. **The masking rule follows the recipient group, not the channel** |
| Attempts | Count, first attempt, last attempt |
| Failure | The RFC 7807 `type` from the adapter's last response (D3 §1.5), and the human-readable `title` |
| Correlation | `correlationId` — the same value that traces the claim across every interface (D3 §1.2) |
| Action | **Resend** (re-renders from the recorded template version), or **Dismiss** with a reason. Both are audited (§6.3) |

#### 6.1.7 Idempotency — a notification is not sent twice

Three independent guards, because the platform receives at-least-once webhooks on I-04, I-08 and I-12 (D3 §1.3) and a retried webhook is the ordinary case, not the exception.

| Layer | Guard |
|---|---|
| **1. The event** | Webhook handlers are idempotent **on the business key, not the delivery id** — `policyNo` (I-04), `requestId` (I-08), `instructionRef` (I-12), `assessmentId` (I-16), exactly as D3 §1.3 requires. A repeated webhook resolves to the domain event that already exists, so no second event is raised and no second outbox row is written. **This is where the guarantee actually comes from** |
| **2. The outbox** | A unique constraint on (`eventId`, `messageCode`, `channel`, `recipientId`). A duplicate insert is a **no-op, not an error** — the caller has already achieved what it asked for, and raising an exception on the correct outcome produces a spurious alert |
| **3. The dispatcher** | A row is claimed with a lease before the adapter is called, and the send record is written in the same transaction as the status transition to `SENT` |

**What the engine guarantees, stated exactly.** *Exactly once per domain event; at-least-once at the transport.* Layer 3 makes a double send vanishingly unlikely but cannot make it impossible — a process that dies between the provider accepting the message and the transaction committing will retry. That residual is acceptable for `IN_APP` and `PUSH` and for every message in A2, because none of them causes an action on receipt. **It would not be acceptable for a payment instruction**, which is why I-11 carries D3 §1.3's `Idempotency-Key` and this engine is not in that path.

#### 6.1.8 Correspondence — the three PDFs

`CLM-LETTER-001`, `CLM-LETTER-002` and `POL-LETTER-001` (A2 §7). The engine renders each from its template plus the claim or policy data, writes the PDF to object storage, and attaches it to the email.

| Rule | Statement |
|---|---|
| **F61-R8** | A letter is **generated once and stored**. A resend attaches the stored bytes. Regenerating would let a settlement notice change between the copy the customer holds and the copy we hold |
| **F61-R9** | The stored PDF is referenced from the claim and is readable in-app (`IN_APP` copy of the same message). Per §2.7 the claim holds the reference, never the bytes |
| **F61-R10** | The benefit-by-benefit table in `CLM-LETTER-001` is data, rendered by the engine from the settlement plan — `BR-MSG-2`, A2 §7.1. Declined lines appear in the same table as paid ones. The engine does not have a mode in which they are separated |

The insurer's legal entity name, logo and correspondence address are **A2 open item A2-01** and are configuration (`config`), not template text.

#### 6.1.9 What F61 does not build

| Not built | Why, and what exists instead |
|---|---|
| **SMS** | No message in A2 uses it (A2 §9). The channel token is honoured by the template model and by the outbox so that adding a message later is content plus a provider, not a change to the engine. **No provider is contracted, no route is configured, and no SMS is sent in MVP 1** |
| **Browser push to the console, and any digest to staff** | **No web push, no desktop notification, and no digest email.** Staff notification is delivered on **`STAFF_INBOX`** (§6.1.2, §6.1.2b, surfaced at §5.23) and, on the two messages A2 §8.1's rule **S-4** names, by `EMAIL`. **What is excluded is the third mechanism and the aggregate one**, and A2 §9 gives the reason for the second: *a digest is the mechanism that trains people to stop reading*, and it would arrive alongside the two alerts that were worth reading. **This row previously excluded staff email outright and it no longer does** — see the note below |
| **The other fourteen staff touch points** | Reference System A carries twenty-two; A2 §8.1 carries eight, chosen on one test — *would a person who is not looking at this claim need to know?* **The count difference is a decision recorded in A2 §9, not an engine limitation.** Adding a ninth is a row in A2 plus a template record here (§6.1.1) |
| **Customer-configurable content or channels** | No preference screen, no opt-out, no quiet hours, no digest frequency. Every message in A2 is transactional and concerns the customer's own claim or policy. Making any of it optional is a business decision nobody has taken, and building the switch before the decision produces a switch nobody knows how to set. **There is no staff preference either** — §6.1.2 gives the reason, and it is stronger |
| **Assessor-to-customer free text** | A2 §9. Information requests are structured (A2 §3.4) so they can be measured and audited |
| **Marketing, renewal and expiry messages** | A2 §9; renewals are out of scope (Framework §7.2) |
| **Template authoring by a non-administrator** | A3 §3.1 grants F61 templates to `ADMIN` at `MASTER` and to nobody else |

> **What this section used to exclude, and why the exclusion is gone rather than amended.** Until this pass **`EMAIL` to a member of staff was excluded outright here, and §6.1.2 had no staff recipient group**. Both were written when in-app and email to a customer were the only channels in the catalogue, and against that catalogue both were right. **A2 v1.1 §8.1 has since specified a `STAFF` family on a `STAFF_INBOX` channel, with `EMAIL` on two of its eight messages, and A2 owns a message's content, channel and wording** (§0.5). **D2 yields**: §6.1.2 carries the channel, §6.1.2b specifies the engine's half of it, and this table now excludes browser push and the digest — which is what A2 §9 excludes too. **`D2-127` is closed**, and A2 records the same item from its side as **A2-06**. **Nothing was built for it**: §6.1.5 to §6.1.7 already carried the outbox, the retry schedule, the idempotency guards and the operator queue, which is exactly why the exclusion was cheap to write and is cheap to remove. **A declared simplification that outlives the reason it was declared is no longer a simplification, it is a contradiction** — and this one had a named consequence, that a claim assigned to somebody on leave was discovered by the ageing report, which is now the thing the bell prevents.

---

### 6.2 Role-based access control with data scope (F62)

**Purpose.** Enforce A3, on every call, from the server, against the data — not against what the client says about itself.

#### 6.2.1 The model

```
User ──< UserRole >── Role ──< Grant >── Permission
                                 │
                                 ├── level      F | R | C     (A3 §0.1)
                                 ├── scope      SELF | ASSIGNED | QUEUE |
                                 │              ALL_CLAIMS | ALL_POLICIES |
                                 │              MASTER | NONE            (A3 §0.3)
                                 └── conditionRule   the A3 §4 rule id, where level = C
```

**A grant is four things, and the fourth is what most systems omit.** A permission without a data scope is a function name with a tick beside it — A3 §0 says so, and the model makes it structurally impossible to record one. `scope` is `NOT NULL`. A grant whose scope is unknown does not exist.

**Conditional grants are data plus code, deliberately split.** Where A3 marks a cell **C**, the grant record carries `conditionRule` — the identifier of the A3 §4 rule (`A3-4.1`, `A3-4.7`, `A3-4.12`…). The *grant* is configuration an administrator can see and audit; the *rule* is code, because every one of A3's fourteen rules needs to read state a configuration table cannot express. Splitting them this way means an administrator can answer "why is this blocked" by reading the grant, and a developer can answer "how is it blocked" by reading one named function.

**Roles.** The four roles in A3 §0.2 are seeded and the console does not offer a fifth. The role record is data rather than an enum in code so that A3's own change-control (A3 §8) is the only thing standing between the pilot and a new role — but adding one is a change to A3 first, and the seeded four cannot be deleted.

**A user may hold more than one role** (A3 §0.2), and in the pilot team that is expected. Holding `ASSESSOR` and `APPROVER` together is permitted; **A3 §4.1 then binds per claim, not per user**, and §6.2.4 is how.

#### 6.2.2 Where enforcement happens

| Layer | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| **API** | **The control.** Every endpoint resolves the acting user's roles and grants **server-side, per request, from current data** and checks both the permission and the scope before anything is read or written. It ignores every role, scope, claim id or user id the client asserts about itself |
| **Query layer** | **Scope is a predicate, not a filter** (A3 §6). A record outside scope is never loaded — so it cannot leak through a row count, a paging total, an error message or a log line. This is the difference between *the user cannot see it* and *the user is not shown it* |
| **UI** | Convenience only. A function the user may not perform is **absent, not disabled** (A3 §0.1). §2.5 says the same from the screen side. Hiding a control is a courtesy; it is never the control |
| **Audit** | Every denial is logged with actor, role, scope, resource and `correlationId` — `BR-AUDIT-5`, A3 §6. A pattern of denials is the earliest signal of either a misconfigured role or a user probing, and neither is visible if refusals are silent |

**The token asserts identity, never authority.** The access token carries `userId` and nothing about what that user may do. Permissions and scopes are resolved from the database on every request.

> **Why not put roles in the token, which is faster.** Because a role revoked at 10:00 would remain valid until the token expired. In a system where the reason to revoke a grant is usually urgent — a conflict of interest discovered, a leaver, a misconfiguration caught — a fifteen-minute window in which the revocation has not taken effect is precisely the window that matters. The cost is one indexed read per request.

#### 6.2.3 Data scope, resolved

| Scope | Predicate applied at the query layer | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `SELF` | `claim.claimantUserId = :actor` for claims; `policy.memberIds ∋ :actorMemberId` for policies | **A3 §4.3**: a customer sees claims **they submitted**. A claim submitted by another member on the same policy is not visible, even to the policyholder. Remaining limits (F25) are shown as **amounts only**, never itemised by who consumed them — the amount is not private, the consumption pattern is |
| `ASSIGNED` | `claim.assigneeUserId = :actor` | |
| `QUEUE` | `claim.queueId ∈ (queues the actor belongs to)` — assigned or unassigned | An assessor sees **their own queue and their unit**. MVP 1 has exactly **one** queue and one unit (Framework S-11), so today this predicate resolves one row of configuration. It is written as a set membership anyway, because S-11 is named as *the first simplification to reverse* and a hard-coded single queue would have to be found and unpicked when it is |
| `ALL_CLAIMS` | No claim predicate; **A3 §4.11's field-level redaction still applies to `ADMIN`** | |
| `ALL_POLICIES` | No policy predicate | A materially smaller grant than `ALL_CLAIMS`: policy data carries no clinical detail (A3 §0.3) |
| `MASTER` | Configuration tables only | Contains no personal data |
| `NONE` | The function does not exist for this role | Not an empty result — a 404-shaped absence |

**Redaction is not a scope.** A3 §4.11 lets an administrator read a claim's *operational* record and bars them from its clinical detail — diagnosis, ICD-10, condition class, cost-line item names, document images. That is enforced as **field-level suppression at the query layer, in the same place as the scope predicate**, so the values are never loaded into a response object that something else might serialise. And the access itself is logged (`BR-AUDIT-4`).

#### 6.2.4 The three rules that are not a simple grant

**A3 §4.1 — segregation of duties, per claim**

| Aspect | Implementation |
|---|---|
| The check | At the moment `APPROVE` or `REJECT` is attempted on a claim, the server reads that claim's **processing trail** (§6.3) and denies if the acting user appears as the actor on any F47, F48 or F49 event |
| What it does **not** check | The session's roles (holding both is legal); the assignment field (an assignment can be reassigned, and the trail cannot); a per-user flag |
| When | **At the click, not at page render.** The trail can change while an approver has the claim open, and a control that was enabled when the page loaded must still fail on submit |
| Message | `CLM-CONSOLE-005` |
| Audit | Logged as a denial with `outcome = DENIED` and the rule id (§6.3) |

> A3 §4.1 is the rule that will be argued about in a three-person pilot team. The specification's answer is that the relief valve is the auto-approval threshold (A3 §4.7, D1 B-03 — 2,000,000 VND), not a weakening of segregation on the claims large enough to have needed review.

**A3 §4.12 — no self-assessment, no related-party assessment**

Two halves, deliberately different in kind, because one is detectable and one is not.

| Half | Implementation |
|---|---|
| **Automatic — ID match** | On open, and again on every state-changing action, the acting user's `idNumber` is compared against the claim's **insured member, claimant and beneficiary** ID numbers (Framework §4.4 models all three separately). A match is a **hard block**: the action is refused, the claim is returned to the queue, `CLM-CONSOLE-011` is shown, and the event is logged with the rule id |
| **Attested — declaration** | On first opening a claim, an assessor or approver is prompted to declare any other relationship — spouse, parent, child, colleague. Declaring **returns the claim to the queue** and writes a declaration record on the claim (actor, timestamp, relationship type, free-text note). `CLM-CONSOLE-012` |
| **A data requirement this creates** | The user record must carry `idNumber` (§6.2.6, U6). A staff directory usually does not hold one, and this is the only reason we need it. It is personal data: it is stored, never displayed on a list screen, never written to an application log, and never leaves the deployment boundary |
| **An honest limit** | The declaration is attested, not verified. Its value is that it is **recorded** — a claim for a spouse under a different surname and ID passes every automatic test, and A3 §4.12 says so in as many words. Without the automatic half the most obvious conflict is unguarded; without the attested half the control is theatre |

**A3 §4.7 and A3 §4.9 — the two-person controls**

Both are implemented by the **same mechanism**, because they are the same shape: an action whose blast radius is far wider than one claim.

```
PendingChange:  requestedBy → (a second administrator) → confirmedBy → applied
```

| Aspect | Implementation |
|---|---|
| The record | A `PendingChange` holding: change type, target, **value before**, **value after**, `requestedBy`, `requestedAt`, `confirmedBy`, `confirmedAt`, `status` (`PENDING` / `CONFIRMED` / `REFUSED` / `LAPSED`) |
| Nothing happens on request | The threshold is unchanged and the import is uncommitted until confirmation. `CLM-CONSOLE-008` tells the requester the change is waiting and names who requested it and when |
| The requester may not confirm | Checked on `confirmedBy ≠ requestedBy`, not on role. `CLM-CONSOLE-009` |
| Both identities are audited | One audit entry naming **both**, with before and after values — A3 §4.7 states this explicitly (§6.3) |
| Expiry | A pending change **lapses after 24 hours**. **Proposed** — no source sets one. A request left open indefinitely is confirmed later by someone who has forgotten what it was for |
| **A3 §4.7 specific — threshold** | The new threshold takes effect for claims **registered after** confirmation, never retrospectively. The same reasoning as A3 §4.14 for the `in_network` flag: a retrospective change would make the same claim settle differently depending on when the chain was re-run, and `BR-TRACK-4` re-runs the chain |
| **A3 §4.9 specific — import commit** | The pending change is bound to the validated result by `importId`. **If the file or the validation result changes, the pending change is void** and a fresh request is required — otherwise the second administrator confirms a validation they never saw. `BR-IMP-1` (nothing written before commit) and `BR-IMP-2` (no partial import) are unchanged by this; the two-person rule sits on top of them |

**A3 §4.8 — no user may modify their own roles.** A simple guard, listed here because it is the fourth non-trivial rule and omitting it would make privilege escalation a single click. Checked as `targetUserId ≠ :actor` on every role-assignment write, including through any bulk path. *(new A2 item needed — **D2-88**)*.

#### 6.2.5 Session, token lifetime and re-authentication

**Every number in this table is a proposal.** No document in this set specifies a session lifetime. Open item **D2-84**.

| Setting | Console | Mobile app | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Authentication | Username + password | Phone + OTP (F21) | Cited — F21 |
| Access token lifetime | 15 minutes | 15 minutes | **Proposed** |
| Refresh token lifetime | 8 hours sliding, 12 hours absolute | 30 days sliding, device-bound | **Proposed** |
| Idle timeout | 30 minutes | None | **Proposed** |
| Concurrent sessions | Permitted, unlimited | Permitted, one per registered device | **Proposed** |
| Revocation | Immediate — permissions resolve per request (§6.2.2), so a role change binds on the next call. Explicit logout revokes the refresh token | Same | **Proposed** |
| Step-up re-authentication | Required before: changing the auto-approval threshold, confirming a pending change (A3 §4.7, A3 §4.9), committing an import, and changing one's own password | Required before changing the payout account (A3 §4.5) | **Proposed** |

**Why step-up at all, on four actions and no others.** Each of the four moves money or moves the boundary of who may move money, and each is reachable from an unattended, already-authenticated console session. Re-authentication is the cheapest available control against a walked-away-from screen, and applying it more widely would train users to type their password without reading why.

`AUTH-VAL-006`† (session expired) and `AUTH-VAL-007`† (re-authentication required) do not exist in A2 and are requested in §6.5.
