### 6.3 Audit logging (F63)

**Purpose.** Record every decision and every data edit, in JSON, so that what happened to a claim — and who caused it — is answerable afterwards without inference.

**Who may read it** — A3 §5. `ASSESSOR` and `APPROVER` read the processing trail of claims in their scope (F53); `ADMIN` reads configuration and access events, **not clinical detail** (A3 §4.11), and their reads are themselves logged; **no cross-user report exists in MVP 1**, because no `AUDITOR` role exists (A3 §5, deferred with S-06).

#### 6.3.1 Two stores, one schema — the distinction the rest of this section depends on

| Store | Contents | Readers | Where personal data may appear |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Audit log** | Decisions, data edits, state transitions, access events, denials, configuration changes | Per A3 §5, via F53 and the admin views | **Yes**, in the restricted partition — a before/after pair on an ICD-10 field is clinical by definition, and `BR-AUDIT-2` requires it |
| **Application log** | Request traces, adapter calls, timings, stack traces, health | Engineers, and any log aggregation index | **Never.** Identifiers only — `correlationId`, `claimNo`, `requestId`, `userId`. No name, no ID number, no diagnosis, no cost-line text, no account number, no document content |

**This split is what reconciles `BR-AUDIT-2` with boundary condition BC-1.** `BR-AUDIT-2` requires the old and new value of every edit, and some of those values are clinical. BC-1 requires that identifiable patient data does not enter the project. The resolution is not to weaken either: the values are captured, in a store with A3 §5's access rules over it and field-level redaction for `ADMIN`, and **the application log — the stream that gets shipped to an aggregator, tailed in a terminal and pasted into a ticket — carries no personal data at all.** A system that logs a diagnosis to `stdout` has put it in five places nobody is tracking.

Both stores use the schema below; **the restricted material is the whole of `changes[]` (A14) and every field of a change row**, and it is simply absent from application-log entries.

#### 6.3.2 What is always logged

| # | Category | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **State transitions** | Every edge in D1 §4.1, with `stateFrom`, `stateTo`, actor and reason. Including the two that bypass the assessor: `DOC_PROCESSING → APPROVED` records **the conditions the auto-approval gate was evaluated against** (`BR-AUTO-5`), and `APPROVED → UNDER_ASSESSMENT` records the override (`BR-AUTO-4`) |
| 2 | **Decisions** | Coverage assessment (F47), per-line pay/decline with reason (F46), clinical recommendation confirmed or rejected **with the rejection reason** (F56, `BR-TRACK-6`), settlement plan submitted (F49), approval or return with reason (F50), cancellation with reason |
| 3 | **Data edits** | **One entry per user action, carrying the before and after value of every field that action changed, as a child detail list** (§6.3.3). On every entity — claim, policy, member, benefit schedule, provider master, configuration. **The coverage is unchanged from v0.2 and the grouping is not**: `BR-AUDIT-2` still requires the old and new value of every changed field, and every one is still written; what changes is that seven fields changed by one save produce **one** entry with seven detail rows rather than seven unrelated entries |
| 4 | **Extraction corrections** | The **original extracted value beside the corrected one**, with the per-field confidence and the `requestId` it came from (F46, `BR-DATA-1`, `BR-DATA-2`). See §6.3.4 |
| 5 | **Access to clinical detail** | Every read of a diagnosis, ICD-10 code, condition class, cost-line item name or document image, and every use of the IDP deep link (F36, A3 §4.10) — `BR-AUDIT-4` |
| 6 | **Denied attempts** | Every refusal, with the rule that refused it — `BR-AUDIT-5`, A3 §6 |
| 7 | **Configuration changes** | Including both identities on a two-person confirmation (A3 §4.7, §4.9), and the effective-dated change to the provider master's `in_network` flag (A3 §4.14) |
| 8 | **Interface calls** | Every adapter call and response, per D3 §1.6.3, keyed on the same `correlationId` |
| 9 | **Notification dispatch** | Enqueued, sent, failed, resent, dismissed (§6.1.6) |
| 10 | **Machine steps** | Auto-approval, ledger posting, scheduled reminders, polling — logged with **`SYSTEM` as the actor, never the last human** (`BR-AUDIT-3`). `IDP` and `IMO` likewise appear as actors in their own right (§1.2) |

#### 6.3.3 Field table — audit log entry

*(Register: **B-37** — the schema change, and the most time-sensitive item in this reissue)*

**The unit of an audit entry is a user action, not a field.**

That sentence is the whole of this revision, and it is worth stating why it replaces the opposite convention rather than supplementing it. v0.2's schema carried one `field` / `valueBefore` / `valueAfter` triple per entry, which meant **a single save that touched seven fields produced seven entries with nothing joining them.** `BR-AUDIT-2` was satisfied — every value was recorded — and the result was unreadable: §5.14.1 promises the assessor a processing trail showing "every action on the claim, with who, when, and old → new", and what the schema could deliver was several dozen consecutive rows bearing the same timestamp and the same actor, differing only in a field name. §5.14.5 forbids showing an empty frame, so what the reader received was a wall.

**And the reason had nowhere to live.** We require a reason at six points — returning a claim, cancelling one, declining a cost line, rejecting a clinical recommendation, waiving a document, dismissing a queue item — and the v0.2 schema's `reason` (A28) sat on the same flat entry as `field`, so a reason belonged either to one field's change or to a reason-only entry with nothing binding it to the change it explained. When somebody asks *why was this claim returned*, the answer had to be assembled from two entries that nothing joined. That is `G-B-13` seen from the schema instead of from the screen.

**The fix adds structure and removes nothing.** Every value v0.2 recorded is still recorded, in the same restricted partition, with the same append-only guarantee and the same redaction for `ADMIN`. `causationId` survives and stops being the only thing holding a fan-out together.

> **This is the Part VI half of `V-720`, and `D2-128` is what asked for it.** §5.14.1 specified the console's trail as one row per action in v0.3 and recorded that the entry schema behind it was Part VI's and unedited. **This section is that edit**, and D1's `BR-AUDIT-2` remains to be restated — **D2-117**, which is `D2-128`'s remaining half.

> **This is a schema change to an append-only store, and that is why it is in this reissue rather than the next one.** Before any code is written it costs a table definition. Afterwards it costs a migration of the one table in the system that is, by design, the hardest to migrate — no updates, no deletes, and a hash chain over its rows (§6.3.6). **On this row the timing of the decision matters more than the content of it.**

**The parent entry — one per action.**

| # | Field | Type | Source | Req | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | `eventId` | `text(36)` | `system` | M | UUIDv4. The entry's own identity |
| A2 | `occurredAt` | `datetime` | `system` | M | ISO-8601 with offset, `Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh` — §2.3, D3 §1.2. Stored UTC. **One value for the whole action**, not one per changed field |
| A3 | `correlationId` | `text(36)` | `system` | M | **`X-Correlation-Id` from D3 §1.2 — the same value, unchanged.** One claim's journey across four systems is reconstructable from this field alone, and that is only true because the adapters propagate it rather than minting their own |
| A4 | `causationId` | `text(36)` | `system` | O | The `eventId` that caused this one. **Proposed** — not in D3. It joins *actions* to each other where one fans out into six; it is no longer doing the job of joining a field to its siblings, which A14 now does |
| A5 | `actorType` | `enum(ActorType)` | `system` | M | `CUST` · `ASSESSOR` · `APPROVER` · `ADMIN` · `SYSTEM` · `IDP` · `IMO` — §1.2. **`SYSTEM`, `IDP` and `IMO` are actors, not attributions to a human** |
| A6 | `actorId` | `text(20)` | `system` | C | Mandatory where A5 is a human actor; empty for `SYSTEM`, `IDP`, `IMO` |
| A7 | `actorRoles` | `text(60)` | `system` | C | The roles held **at the moment of the action**, not as they stand now |
| A8 | `sessionId` | `text(36)` | `system` | C | |
| A9 | `sourceIp` | `text(45)` | `system` | C | Human actors only |
| A10 | `action` | `enum(AuditAction)` | `system` | M | `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` — §2.6. `CLAIM_APPROVED`, `CLAIM_RETURNED`, `LINE_DECLINED`, `EXTRACTION_CORRECTED`, `CLAIM_FIELDS_EDITED`, `PERMISSION_DENIED`, `CLINICAL_DETAIL_READ`, `THRESHOLD_CHANGED`. **The value names what the person did, and it is what §5.14.1's trail renders as its description column** |
| A11 | `entityType` / `entityId` | `text(30)` / `text(40)` | `system` | M | `CLAIM`/`CLM-26-000417`, `POLICY`/`POL-26-004417`, `CONFIG`/`AUTO_APPROVAL_THRESHOLD`. **The entity the action was performed on**; a change row may name a different, subordinate one (C1) |
| A12 | `claimNo` | `text(20)` | `system` | C | **§2.9's canonical width.** Denormalised onto every claim-related entry so the trail can be read without a join. Format per Framework §7.5, never parsed — and **never truncated**: an audit entry that clipped the event suffix would attribute a decision to the wrong event (§2.11 UI-19) |
| A13 | `stateFrom` / `stateTo` | `enum(ClaimState)` | `system` | C | A1 §5.1. Mandatory on a transition |
| **A14** | **`changes[]`** | **`derived` — the child table below** | `system` | **C** | **Mandatory where A10 is an editing action; empty otherwise.** One element per field the action changed. **Restricted partition — the whole array.** `V-630` |
| **A15** | **`changeCount`** | `int` | `system` | C | Derived, stored. **Held so that a trail can render *"7 trường đã thay đổi"* without reading the restricted partition**, which matters because `ADMIN` may see that an edit happened and not what was edited (A3 §4.11) |
| **A16** | **`reason`** | `textarea(2000)` | **`user`** | C | **Its own column, on the action, carrying what the person typed.** §2.9's free-text reason width, so the log holds what the screen accepted. **Mandatory on: a return, a cancellation, a line decline, a clinical-recommendation rejection, a document waiver, a queue dismissal, an auto-approval override, and any correction of a value the customer declared.** `V-631`. **This is a reason for the *action*; a per-line rationale that belongs to one changed value goes on the change row (C7)** |
| A17 | `outcome` | `enum(AuditOutcome)` | `system` | M | `ALLOWED` · `DENIED` · `FAILED` |
| A18 | `problemType` | `text(120)` | `system` | C | **The RFC 7807 `type` URI from D3 §1.5**, where A17 is `FAILED`. Deliberately the `type` and not the status: D3 §1.3 has two different `409`s that mean opposite things, and a log that recorded only the status could not tell them apart afterwards either |
| A19 | `ruleId` | `text(20)` | `system` | C | Where A17 is `DENIED` — the A3 §4 rule that refused it |
| A20 | `interfaceId` | `text(6)` | `system` | C | `I-05`, `I-09`, `I-11`… |
| A21 | `idempotencyKey` | `text(36)` | `system` | C | The `Idempotency-Key` sent or received, per D3 §1.3 |
| A22 | `ruleVersion` | `text(20)` | `system` | C | The adjudication configuration in force |
| A23 | `kbVersion` | `text(20)` | `system` | C | Clinical knowledge-base version in force — `BR-KB-4`, `BR-KB-5` |
| A24 | `snapshotId` | `text(36)` | `snapshot` | C | The policy snapshot the decision was taken against (D1 §7.2) |
| A25 | `messageCode` | `text(20)` | `system` | C | The A2 code shown to the actor, where one was |

**The change row — one per changed field, inside `changes[]`.**

| # | Field | Type | Source | Req | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | `target` | `text(40)` | `system` | C | **Which subordinate record the field is on**, where the action touched a collection — `costLine/7`, `event/2`, `checklistItem/T1-02`. Empty where the field is on A11's entity itself. **Without this, an action that edits seven cost lines produces seven rows that all say `amount`** |
| C2 | `field` | `text(60)` | `system` | M | The field name, in the payload's own naming (§2.6) |
| C3 | `valueBefore` | `text(500)` | `system` | M | **Restricted partition** — `BR-AUDIT-2`. `null` is written as the literal null and is distinct from an empty string |
| C4 | `valueAfter` | `text(500)` | `system` | M | **Restricted partition** |
| C5 | `extractedValue` | `text(500)` | `idp:I-09` | C | **Restricted partition.** The original extraction value, carried beside the correction — §6.3.4. **Per field, which is where it always belonged**: an action correcting three extracted values carries three of them |
| C6 | `extractionConfidence` | `pct` | `idp:I-09` | C | Basis points, per §2.3 |
| C7 | `fieldReason` | `text(500)` | `user` | C | **A rationale attached to this change alone**, where the screen collected one per line rather than one per action — a cost line's decline rationale is the case that matters (§5.6, A5 §6.3). **Distinct from A16**, and both may be present: an action may have one reason and one of its lines another |
| C8 | `sourceRequestId` | `text(36)` | `system` | C | `requestId` (I-09) or `assessmentId` (I-16) the value came from |

**Four properties of this schema, and each has a consequence if it is got wrong.**

1. **A change row never exists without a parent.** It is not a table with a foreign key that could be orphaned; it is a nested array on one JSON object, written in one insert (below). `V-630`.
2. **The whole array is in the restricted partition, not selected fields of it.** A change row's *field name* can be as clinical as its value — a row naming `icd10Code` reveals that a diagnosis was edited. Redaction for `ADMIN` (A3 §4.11) removes `changes[]` entirely and leaves `changeCount`, which is why A15 is stored rather than computed.
3. **One entry, one insert, one JSON object — including its array.** Nothing is updated. Nothing is deleted. The hash chain of §6.3.6 covers the object with its array inside it, so a change row cannot be added to a past action without breaking the chain.
4. **A15 and A16 are readable without the restricted partition and are what a trail renders by default.** §5.14.1's processing trail shows the time, the actor, the action, the reason and *"n trường đã thay đổi"*, and the change rows open on demand through §5.14.4's *Xem chi tiết mục* — which is exactly the shape the reference arrived at, and the reason it is readable.

> **`V-552`'s redaction is unchanged in effect and simpler to implement.** For `ADMIN` the trail showed operational rows only and clinical rows were withheld with a visible note; it now withholds `changes[]` and keeps `changeCount`, so the note says *how many* were withheld rather than merely *that some were*.

> **`FOR D1` — `BR-AUDIT-2`.** The rule reads that every change records its before and after value. **That is still true and should be restated as grouped by action**, so that D1 and this schema say the same thing. A rule that reads as one-entry-per-field and a schema that is one-entry-per-action will be reconciled by whoever writes the code, in whichever direction is easier that afternoon. Carried as **D2-117**, a correction owed to D1, and it is the open half of `D2-128`.

> **`FOR D3` — §1.6.3.** Where an audit entry is emitted across an interface, its shape changes. Carried as **D2-118**.

> **The enum `AuditAction` gains members and needs registering.** §6.5.2 already lists `AuditAction` among the sets with no home; the set is now larger and its values name user actions rather than field mutations. It stays inside **D2-88**, and this is the reason that item should not be allowed to drift: three parts now depend on it.

#### 6.3.4 The original extraction value beside the corrected one

`BR-DATA-1` says the extraction result is never overwritten; `BR-DATA-2` says corrections go to the claim's own copy and the pair stays comparable; A3 §3.3 says **nobody may edit the raw extraction result, not even an administrator**. F63's part in that is **C5, C6 and C8 on the change row**: a correction carries `valueBefore` (the value on the claim, which may itself already be a correction), `valueAfter`, **and `extractedValue`** — what IDP actually returned, with its confidence and its `requestId`. **They sit on the change row rather than on the action** because one save may correct three extracted values, and one `extractedValue` on the parent could only ever describe one of them.

**Why the third value is not redundant.** After two corrections, `valueBefore` is another human's edit, not IDP's output. Only `extractedValue` answers *what did the machine read* — and that question is what makes extraction accuracy measurable against SC-02, and what makes the auto-approval threshold tunable (D1 §7.1). A log that recorded only before-and-after would lose it on the second edit.

#### 6.3.5 What must never be logged

| Never | Instead |
|---|---|
| **Document images or bytes**, in either store | The object-storage **reference** (§2.7). The claim holds a reference and so does the log |
| **A signed URL** for a document or an IDP deep link | The object id, or `requestId`. A signed URL in a log line is a credential with a 15-minute life (A3 §4.10) sitting in a file with a much longer one |
| **Any clinical detail in the application log** | Nothing. Not the diagnosis, not the ICD-10 code, not the condition class, not a cost-line item name, not a prescription line. Under boundary condition **BC-1** the project holds only anonymised documents, and the way a project stops being able to make that claim is a stack trace that printed a payload |
| **OTP codes, passwords, tokens, HMAC signatures** | The fact of the event and its outcome |
| **A full bank account number** | Masked to the last four, everywhere — the same masking A2 applies as `{maskedAccount}` |
| **A full ID number in the application log** | The `memberId`, which is ours and means nothing outside the system |
| **The raw body of an inbound webhook, unredacted** | D3 §1.6.3 requires the adapter to record the request and response; the recording is written to the **restricted** partition, with document content and clinical fields elided |

#### 6.3.6 Append-only, and how that is actually enforced

| Control | Implementation |
|---|---|
| No update, no delete | The application's database role holds `INSERT` and `SELECT` on the audit tables and **nothing else** — `BR-AUDIT-1`. This is a grant, not a convention; a convention is one careless migration away from being untrue |
| No administrator exception | A3 §5: no role, including `ADMIN`, may edit or delete an entry. There is no screen, no endpoint and no support tool that can |
| Tamper evidence | Each entry carries the hash of the previous entry **for the same claim**, chained. **Proposed** — no source requires it. It is a few lines of code now and it is the difference between "we believe the log is complete" and "we can show it is" |
| Corrections | An erroneous entry is **never edited**. A compensating entry is appended, referencing the original by `causationId` |

#### 6.3.7 Retention — and the gap, stated rather than filled

**D1 NFR-8 records the retention of claim data and audit as *unset and unowned*.** It is explicit that no B-decision exists for it, that A3-05 covers audit entries and access logs only and is itself open with ISMS, and that a new B-item is needed before release. **This document does not invent one.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **What the system does by default** | **Nothing is deleted.** No purge job is built, no time-to-live is configured on any table or object-storage bucket, and no archive tier is scheduled. Audit entries, claim records, generated PDFs and stored documents persist for the life of the environment |
| **Why that is the right default here** | Under BC-1 the data is anonymised, under BC-2 there are no real customers and under BC-3 no real money — so the risk of keeping it is low, and the risk of deleting evidence during a pilot whose whole purpose is measurement is not. More to the point, a purge job written against an unowned policy is worse than none: it would delete on a schedule nobody agreed and create the appearance of a retention control the business had never set |
| **What is built anyway, because retrofitting it is expensive** | Audit entries are partitioned by month and claim records carry a closure date, so **a retention policy, once set, can be applied without re-modelling anything**. §6.3.6's hash chain is per claim rather than global for the same reason — purging one claim must not break the chain over every other. **The partitioning and the per-claim chaining are proposals**; the policy they anticipate is not ours to write |
| **Application log retention** | **90 days. Proposed.** This is a separate decision from NFR-8 and can be taken by the development lead, because the application log holds no personal data (§6.3.1) and no evidentiary value |
| **The gap, named** | **NFR-8 needs a B-item opened in D1 §11 (open item D2-82), and A3-05 needs closing by ISMS (open item D2-83).** Neither is a D2 decision, and the system as specified will run without them — it will simply hold everything, forever, which is a position somebody should take knowingly rather than inherit |

---

### 6.4 Non-functional baseline (F64)

**How to read the tables in this section.** Every row carries a **Status**: *Cited* means the number comes from D1 §8, Framework §1.3 or D3 and this document is restating it; **Proposed** means this document is suggesting it and nobody has agreed it yet. An invented target presented as agreed is worse than an open item, so the distinction is on every row rather than in a footnote.

#### 6.4.1 Performance

| # | Target | Value | Status | Source / note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | Claim submission response to the customer | 3 s, excluding upload | Cited | D1 NFR-1 |
| P2 | Extraction turnaround, complete package | Median ≤ 5 min, p95 ≤ 30 min | Cited | D1 NFR-2. *"The one the customer experiences as the product"* |
| P3 | Clinical assessment turnaround | Median ≤ 2 min, p95 ≤ 10 min; a claim waits **at most 30 min**, then falls through to `BR-TRACK-5` | Cited | D1 NFR-2a |
| P4 | Adjudication computation | ≤ 2 s per claim | Cited | D1 NFR-3 |
| P5 | **Claim cycle time — submit to approved settlement** | **Median ≤ 1 working day, for complete outpatient claims** | Cited | Framework SC-04. See the definition below |
| P6 | Console page render, first meaningful paint | p95 ≤ 2 s | **Proposed** | |
| P7 | Work-list search and filter (F42) | p95 ≤ 1.5 s at 500 claims/day × 90 days retained | **Proposed** | Sized from NFR-6 |
| P8 | Claim detail open, including the pinned snapshot (F45) | p95 ≤ 2 s | **Proposed** | |
| P9 | Dashboard (F54) | p95 ≤ 3 s | **Proposed** | Counters may be computed on a schedule rather than live if this binds |
| P10 | Audit trail query for one claim (F53) | p95 ≤ 2 s | **Proposed** | |
| P11 | Notification enqueue → dispatch | p95 ≤ 60 s for `IN_APP`, `PUSH` and **`STAFF_INBOX`**; ≤ 5 min for `EMAIL` | **Proposed** | **`STAFF_INBOX` takes `IN_APP`'s target and not `EMAIL`'s**, because it is a local write on the same path. The number is what makes the bell worth having: **a claim-assignment notice that arrives minutes late is a notice that arrives after the assignee has already refreshed the work list**, which is the mechanism it was added to replace (§5.23) |
| P12 | Correspondence PDF generation | ≤ 10 s | **Proposed** | |

**What "complete outpatient claim" means for SC-04, stated so the measure is computable.** An outpatient claim on which **every document at requirement level *required* (A4 §6) was present at submission** and **no information request was raised**. Claims that entered `PENDING_INFO` are excluded from the median, because the clock then includes the customer's response time, which the platform does not control.

> **What P5 actually rests on.** For the sub-threshold population it rests on auto-approval firing — which requires the clinical assessment to have completed and returned nothing (D1 §5.8, condition 2). **Framework RK-13 records that if F37 is not built, condition 2 is unsatisfiable and auto-approval never fires**, at which point SC-04 rests on assessor throughput alone. That is a fail-safe posture and it is the right one, but it means P5 is not independent of a confirmation that is still open (C-IDP-09).

#### 6.4.2 Availability and degraded operation

| # | Target | Value | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | Availability, business hours | 99.5% | Cited — D1 NFR-4 |
| A2 | Business hours | 08:00–18:00 ICT, Monday to Saturday | **Proposed** — NFR-4 names business hours without defining them |
| A3 | Planned maintenance | Outside business hours, announced | **Proposed** |
| A4 | Recovery point / recovery time | RPO ≤ 15 min, RTO ≤ 4 h | **Proposed** |

**Degraded operation.** The governing rule is the same in every row and it is not negotiable: **an operational failure produces an operational state and an operator queue, never a claim outcome** (§2.10, D1 §4.3, A2 rule M-6). Nothing below ever produces a `DECLINED`.

> **This table is rewritten in v0.2, and the rewrite is the plainest statement of what the architecture change cost.** v0.1 carried two rows where there is now one, and the second of them read: *"J2 is unaffected. Policies already in the Policy Data Store are what claims read, and the store is not InsureMO."* **There is no store.** An InsureMO outage now stops every new claim at registration — which is the price of deleting a system, stated where an operator will meet it rather than only where an architect will.

| Unreachable | What stops | **What still works** | Customer sees |
|---|---|---|---|
| **BnK IDP** (I-07, I-08, I-09, I-15, I-16) | New packages cannot be submitted for extraction; results cannot be pulled; the clinical assessment does not run | Claims submit and documents upload normally. The claim holds in `DOC_PROCESSING`; after D3 §1.3's retries are exhausted it moves to **`EXTRACTION_ERROR`** — a recoverable branch with an operator queue — and is resubmitted when IDP returns. **Every claim already extracted is fully workable**: correction, coverage assessment, calculation, settlement plan, approval, payment. The clinical track falls through at 30 minutes per NFR-2a with `CLM-CONSOLE-015`, and **auto-approval simply does not fire** | `SYS-ERR-001`, which reads as a progress update — because from the customer's side it is one |
| **InsureMO** (I-01 … I-06) | **J1 stops entirely** — no catalogue, no quote, no application, no issuance. **And J2 stops at the door**: no new claim can be registered, because registration needs the coverage read and the benefit tree (§5.2.2). Payout-account verification is unaffected — the account is ours (F58) — but the insured's name and card number on §5.20 fall back to the snapshot. My cover (§4.4) and the claim form's policy and member pickers (§4.5) read live and degrade to the last successfully loaded data, marked stale | **Every claim already registered is unaffected, and this is exactly what P-02 bought.** The snapshot is on the claim, so assessment, extraction review, the coverage assessment, the rule chain, the limit ledger, the settlement plan, approval, payment and closure all run to completion. The ledger is ours (Framework §6.1) and touches InsureMO nowhere. Claims awaiting registration hold in `SUBMITTED` and retry. **I-06 claim registration is fire-and-forget and optional**; it queues and retries, and no claim ever waits on it | `SYS-ERR-002`. In the console, `CLM-CONSOLE-007` where no schedule can be retrieved — which instructs the assessor **not to proceed** |
| **The payout-account verification service** | Verification of new or changed accounts, and therefore **settlement plan submission** (V-593) and **payment** (A3 §4.6) on the claims affected | Everything else, including assessment and calculation on those same claims. The failure goes to the operator queue (§5.20.7) | **Nothing.** A verification the service could not perform is not the customer's error to fix — A2 rule M-7 |
| **Object storage** | Document capture and upload | Everything not involving a new document. A claim cannot be submitted with documents while it is down | `SYS-ERR-003` |
| **Finance stub** (I-11, I-12) | Payment instruction and confirmation | Everything up to and including approval. The claim holds in `PAYMENT_IN_PROGRESS` with an operator queue and **does not close** — D1 §4.5 gates closure on money having moved | `PAY-NOTIF-001` stands; nothing new is sent |
| **Notification engine** (§6.1) | Delivery | **Everything.** F61-R5: no claim state depends on a notification | Nothing. The in-app record is written from the outbox when dispatch resumes |

#### 6.4.3 PII handling under the four boundary conditions

Framework §9.4 defers legal and data-protection review **only while all four boundary conditions hold**. F64's job is to say what the platform does about each — and, where the control is a process rather than a system control, to say that rather than imply otherwise.

| BC | Condition | What the platform does | Honest limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| **BC-1** | No identifiable patient data | Document processing stays **inside the deployment boundary** (NFR-7, P-07) — no document and no extracted field reaches an external service. Clinical detail is suppressed for `ADMIN` at the query layer (A3 §4.11) and every read of it is logged (`BR-AUDIT-4`). **The application log carries no personal data at all** (§6.3.1). Documents are referenced, never embedded (§2.7) | **The platform cannot tell whether a document is anonymised.** BC-1 is enforced at ground-truth handover as an acceptance step, not by software — Framework RK-05 says so, and claiming a system control here would be false assurance |
| **BC-2** | No real customers | Accounts are created by phone + OTP (F21) and every account is a named tester | **Registration is open by design.** BC-2 is held by not publishing the app. **Proposed:** a configuration allow-list of permitted tester phone numbers, enforced at F21 — it converts a process control into a system one for close to no cost, and it is the cheapest of the four to make real. Open item **D2-87** |
| **BC-3** | No real money | Payment instructions go to the I-11 stub; premium collection to the I-13 mock (D3 §0.1 marks I-13 Provisional **because of BC-3**, not because a vendor has to answer). **Proposed:** a persistent, non-dismissible environment banner in every non-production console stating that no real money moves | **Framework §9.4 attaches a release gate here.** Declared simplification S-17 — the BHYT share is captured but not deducted — is acceptable *only* while BC-3 holds. The first real payment is the gate, not a backlog item |
| **BC-4** | Not offered as insurance | No public distribution; no marketing or re-engagement messages exist to send (A2 §9) | A distribution control, not a platform one |

**PII handling regardless of the boundary conditions**, because these are cheap now and awkward later: TLS 1.2 minimum on every hop including local development (D3 §1.1); encryption at rest for the database and object storage (**proposed** — no source specifies it; open item **D2-86**); bank account numbers masked to the last four in every display, every message and every log; ID numbers stored but never rendered on a list screen; and no personal data in any metric or dashboard dimension.

#### 6.4.4 Logging and observability

**Three streams, kept apart** — §6.3.1 defines the first two; metrics are the third and carry **counts and latencies only, never an identifier**, so that a dashboard can be shared without a data-protection question.

| Metric | Serves |
|---|---|
| Claim counts by state, and ageing from submission | F54, D1 §8.1 |
| Extraction turnaround, median and p95 | NFR-2 |
| Clinical assessment turnaround, and the fall-through count at 30 minutes | NFR-2a, `BR-TRACK-5` |
| Adjudication computation time | NFR-3 |
| **Auto-approval rate, and for claims that did not auto-approve, the condition that failed** | D1 §5.8. Which of the **three** fails is the number that tells the business whether the threshold, the clinical track or **the term layer** is the constraint. **From v0.5 the third answer exists and it is the one nobody has a baseline for** (§5.11.4) |
| **Agreement rate** — recommendations confirmed vs rejected | **SC-09** and `BR-TRACK-6`. **The target itself is open (B-16)**, and below it the clinical track reverts to advisory mode. The measure is built from day one whether or not the target exists |
| Extraction field accuracy, corrected vs original | SC-01, SC-02 — computable only because of §6.3.4 |
| Notification dispatch success and failure by channel | §6.1 |
| Interface error rate **by RFC 7807 `type`**, not by status | D3 §1.5 — the two `409`s again |
| Denied permission attempts, by rule | A3 §6, `BR-AUDIT-5` |

**Alerting.** An alert is raised on: retry exhaustion on any adapter (D3 §1.3), a claim in `EXTRACTION_ERROR` beyond **60 minutes** (**proposed**), a claim in `PAYMENT_IN_PROGRESS` beyond **1 working day** (**proposed**), any notification in the failure queue, and any `5xx` rate above **1% over 5 minutes** (**proposed**). Each adapter exposes a health check.

Everything below marked **Proposed** is open item **D2-85**.

| | Support | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Mobile app | Android and iOS, current and one prior major version | Cited — D1 NFR-9 |
| Console browsers | Chrome and Edge, current and one prior major version; Firefox current; Safari current | **Proposed** |
| Console minimum viewport | 1366 × 768 | **Proposed** — the work list and the extraction-review split view (F46) are the two screens that set it |
| Console offline | Not supported | **Proposed** |

#### 6.4.6 Concurrency

| # | Target | Value | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | Concurrent assessors supported | 20 | Cited — D1 NFR-5 |
| C2 | Claims per day supported | 500 | Cited — D1 NFR-6 |
| C3 | Concurrent adjudications against one member's limit counters | No fixed limit; correctness is guaranteed by optimistic versioning | Cited — D1 §5.9, Framework §4.4 |

**The limit ledger's optimistic versioning is D1's.** Counters carry a version; two claims for the same member adjudicating against the same annual limit simultaneously is a real race, not a theoretical one; posting is two-phase, provisional at calculation and final at approval. **What this document has to specify is what the console does when it loses that race**, because D1 defines the mechanism and not the screen behaviour.

| Situation | What the console does |
|---|---|
| **The calculation loses the race** (a `version-conflict` on posting — D3 §1.5's second `409` shape) | The provisional posting is discarded and the rule chain is **re-run once, automatically, against the fresh counters**. The assessor is shown the recomputed settlement with **the lines that changed flagged at the field**, and must re-confirm before submitting |
| Why not simply fail | Because the second claim's numbers are legitimately different. The other claim consumed part of the limit and this claim's payable really has changed. An error message would tell the assessor to do by hand what the engine has just done correctly |
| Why not simply save | Because the assessor submitted a settlement plan for figures they had read. Silently substituting different ones is how an approver ends up approving a number nobody looked at — the same failure D1 §3.2.5's claim lock exists to prevent from the other direction |
| **A second consecutive conflict** | Stop. The assessor is told the limit changed while they were working and asked to reload — *(new A2 item needed — **D2-88**)*. Retrying indefinitely under contention produces a screen that never settles |
| **The claim lock** (D1 §3.2.5) | On submission for approval the whole claim is read-only — amounts, coverage decisions, document actions, and any fresh extraction request alike. The lock releases on approval or on return, **never by the assessor**. A version conflict cannot occur on a locked claim, because nothing on it can be recalculated |
| **Two assessors, one claim** | Prevented by scope, not by locking: `ASSIGNED` (A3 §0.3) means one assignee. An assessor who opens a claim assigned to someone else sees it read-only |
| **Two administrators, one configuration record** | Last write wins, with a version check — the loser is told the record changed and shown the current value. The two-person controls in §6.2.4 are a separate mechanism and are not affected |

### 6.6 Validation rules

The rules §6.1 and §6.2 cite by identifier, defined once here — Part VIII §8.1. **Ten identifiers are allocated out of the `V-601 … V-699` range.** §6.3's audit log entry cites **two**, and that is a change from v0.2, which said it cited none. The reason is §6.3.3's schema: a nested structure has an invariant a flat row did not have, and an invariant nobody wrote down is an invariant the first refactor removes.

**The last column does not mean the same thing on every row, and that is the point of this paragraph.** These are **record schemas, not screens** (§6.0). Where the record is edited by an administrator on an F55 screen — the notification template, the user record — the rule fails at a person and raises a message, and the message is allocated in Part V. Where the record is written by a migration or by the platform — the grant table — **there is nobody to tell**, and the honest entry in *On failure* is a **behaviour**: the write is rejected and the rejection is logged. A behaviour in that column is not a missing message.

| # | Rule | Enforced | On failure |
|---|---|---|---|
| **V-601** | **A template's message code must already exist in A2**, in the format `<AREA>-<TYPE>-<NNN>` (A2 §0.2). The engine never creates a message code; A2 does, and a template for a code A2 does not carry is a sentence nobody wrote | Both — format on the client, existence on the server | *(new A2 item needed — **D2-88**)* |
| **V-602** | **A template's channel must be one A2 lists against that message code.** Channel is a property of the message, not of the engine or the recipient (A2 M-9, §6.1.2) | Both | *(new A2 item needed — **D2-88**)* |
| **V-603** | **A subject line is mandatory where the channel is `EMAIL` and must be empty on every other channel** — `EMAIL` is the only channel with a subject to carry | Both | *(new A2 item needed — **D2-88**)* |
| **V-604** | **Every `{placeholder}` in a template body is named rather than positional, and must be in the parameter set the triggering event supplies.** An unknown, positional or unsupplied placeholder is rejected **at save**, never discovered at render time in front of a customer (F61-R2, F61-R4) | Server | *(new A2 item needed — **D2-88**)* |
| **V-610** | **A login name is unique across all users, compared case-insensitively** — `ADMIN` and `admin` are one login and the second is refused. It is immutable after creation (§5.16.1 F1) | Both | Screen: `inline` on a duplicate, per §5.16.1. Write path: rejected, logged |
| **V-611** | **An email address is well-formed and unique across all users** | Both | Screen: message allocated in Part V (F55), §5.16.1 F3. Write path: rejected, logged |
| **V-612** | **An identity document number is mandatory on any user holding `ASSESSOR` or `APPROVER`**, because it is the sole input to A3 §4.12's automatic conflict-of-interest check (V-594, V-502). It is **never rendered on a list screen and never written to an application log** (§6.3.1) | Both | Screen: message allocated in Part V (F55). The non-rendering half raises nothing at all — see below |
| **V-620** | **A grant may name only a function A3 names.** A grant on a function A3 does not list is a defect in this document, not a new permission | Server, and at build time | **Rejected, logged.** The grant table is seeded from A3 as a migration (§6.2.8) and has no screen behind it, so there is nobody to message; the build-time test that asserts the seed matches A3 row for row fails instead |
| **V-630** | **An audit entry whose action is an editing action carries at least one change row, and a change row exists only inside a parent entry.** The write is one insert of one object; there is no path that produces an entry with an empty `changes[]` for an action that changed something, and no path that produces a change row on its own | Server, and at the storage layer | **Rejected, logged.** There is nobody to message — an audit write has no screen behind it (the paragraph above). A rejected audit write is itself an operational alert on S-03, because a claim action that succeeded with no trail is worse than a claim action that failed |
| **V-631** | **The reason column is populated on every action that requires a reason** — the eight listed at §6.3.3 A16 — and the requirement is enforced on the **write of the audit entry**, not only on the screen that collected it. A screen can be bypassed; the audit write cannot | Server | **Rejected, logged**, as V-630. **The action is refused with it** — this is the one audit invariant that blocks the business operation, because an approval returned without a recorded reason is the case the rule exists for |

**V-612 is the one rule here with a half that no message can ever carry.** The mandatory check fails at a person on the F55 screen and raises a message like any other. The prohibition on rendering the number — no list screen, no application log — fails at a code review, at a log-redaction test or not at all, and it is written down here so that it is somebody's rule rather than an assumption the screen and the logger each expect the other to hold.

## Part VII — The claim state machine as an action matrix

D1 §3.2 defines the states and why there is only one machine. This part turns that into the thing a developer actually needs: **for every state, which actions exist, who may perform them, and what each one does to the claim.** It is the single place to check whether a control should be on a screen.

### 7.1 The thirteen states

A1 §5.1 carries the internal Vietnamese labels and is authoritative for them. **The customer-facing status is a different thing and Part IV §4.7 owns it** — thirteen internal states map to ten customer-facing statuses. This table adds only what a developer needs, and its fourth column is copied from Part IV §4.7 rather than restated.

| # | State | Kind | Customer-facing status (Part IV §4.7) | Claim is editable | Ledger position |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `DRAFT` | Customer | *Nháp* | Yes, by the customer | None |
| 2 | `SUBMITTED` | Transitional | *Đã gửi* | No | None |
| 3 | `DOC_PROCESSING` | **Operational** | *Đang xử lý chứng từ* | No | None until the chain runs |
| 4 | `PENDING_INFO` | Customer | *Cần bổ sung chứng từ* | Documents, by the customer; the assessor may still assess and submit (V-514) | Provisional, where a chain run has happened |
| 5 | `EXTRACTION_ERROR` | **Operational** | *Đang xử lý chứng từ* — **never as itself** | Yes, by the assessor | None |
| 6 | `UNDER_ASSESSMENT` | Internal | *Đang thẩm định* | Yes, by the assigned assessor | Provisional, after the first chain run |
| 7 | `PENDING_APPROVAL` | Internal | *Đang thẩm định* — **shown as `UNDER_ASSESSMENT`** | **No — locked** (D1 §3.2.5) | Provisional |
| 8 | `APPROVED` | Outcome | *Đã duyệt* | No | **Final** |
| 9 | `DECLINED` | Outcome | *Từ chối* | No | Provisional reversed; nothing final was ever posted |
| 10 | `PAYMENT_IN_PROGRESS` | **Operational** | *Đang chi trả* | No | Final |
| 11 | `PAID` | Outcome | *Đã chi trả* | No | Final |
| 12 | `CLOSED` | Terminal | *Đã đóng* | No | Final |
| 13 | `CANCELLED` | Terminal | *Đã hủy* | No | Any provisional posting reversed |

**The three states marked Operational are the reason this table has a customer-facing column.** A stalled extraction, an unreachable service and a stalled payment are failures of ours, not decisions about a claim. D1 §4.3 and A2 rule M-6 forbid showing any of them as an outcome. `EXTRACTION_ERROR` in particular **never appears to a customer under any label of its own** — it shows as *Đang xử lý chứng từ*, exactly like `DOC_PROCESSING`, and the timeline entry is `SYS-ERR-001`, which is deliberately written to read as a progress update because from the customer's side it is one.

**`PENDING_APPROVAL` is concealed too, and for a different reason.** It is not an operational failure; it is an internal step. A2 carries no notification for it, and naming an approval stage to a customer exposes the segregation-of-duties structure to no benefit (Part IV §4.7). **`UNDER_ASSESSMENT` is not concealed** — it is *Đang thẩm định*, distinct from *Đang xử lý chứng từ*, and it must be, because `CLM-NOTIF-004` fires on entry to it. A mapping that collapsed the two would fire a notification announcing a change the customer's screen does not show.

**The ledger column is the one most easily got wrong.** Posting is two-phase: provisional when the calculation runs, **final at approval — not at payment** (D1 BR-LEDGER-1, A5 §6.1 step 14, D3 G-2). A failed payment produces a **reversal entry**, never a deletion, and the ledger is not un-finalised (§7.3). Framework §7.1's title for F52 says "final ledger posting"; it is wrong, and Part X carries it as **D2-68**.

### 7.2 The action matrix

Read it as: *in this state, this actor may do this, provided that.* **An action not listed for a state does not exist in that state** — the control is absent, and the server rejects the call. There is no third category of "visible but disabled for business reasons"; a disabled control that a user cannot explain is a support call.

**Columns follow §2.5** — *Who*, *Precondition*, *Effect*, *Message* — with *From* and *To* added, because a transition is what this part is about. **The message has its own column on purpose:** an A2 code buried in a sentence about effects is a code nobody checks.

Two scoping notes. **Actions that only read** — opening a claim, opening a document, exporting the step table — are not transitions and are governed by A3 §2.1 alone; they are not listed here. And the *Who* column is **A3 §2.1's per-feature grid**, not a restatement of who is nearby: where A3 gives a role a dash, the role does not appear.

> **Reduced from the register's B-03, and here is what was left out.** The reference's counter-intake screen accepts **many files at once, each file becoming its own claim**, with the filename taken as the insured's name, automatic assignment, automatic dispatch to extraction and a **copy-claim** control beside it. **We build one claim at a time, with no bulk create and no copy.** Bulk creation from a folder of files is a backlog-clearance tool and pays for itself only where a stock of paper claims exists; copy-claim pays only at a volume of repeat visits a pilot will not reach. **What is not optional is that a route exists at all**: without one, every claim that arrives by paper, by email or by telephone is worked outside the system — no number, no trail, no SLA clock, no report — and a pilot with no counter route does not avoid counter claims, it merely handles them in a spreadsheet. **Both omissions should be declared** in the Framework's simplification register rather than left silent; the register proposes them as `S-26` and `S-27` and **the identifiers are the Framework's to allocate** — the request joins **D2-135**.

> **Reduced from the register's B-44, and here is what was left out.** The reference gates its **intake acceptance** step — a separate human action, with its own status, that a claim must pass before it reaches an assessor. **We have no such step**, because we have one queue and one processing role (declared simplification `S-11`), so there is nothing for an acceptance gate to hand the claim to. What we take from B-44 is its four conditions, applied as **preconditions on registration** — on both routes, the app's and the counter's — so that an empty claim cannot enter the queue by either. What we leave out is the separate acceptance action and the separate status. **Note that on the app route all four conditions were already enforced at capture**; the change there is that they are now also enforced at registration, server-side, which is where V-001 says every rule belongs.

> **The counter-intake screen itself is Part V's and is not written in this reissue.** It is a form entered from the work list, collecting the insured through S-04's search, the loss type from `enum(lossType)`'s **twelve** values, the event dates, the claimant block of §3.2.10, the amount claimed, the intake source, the request-received date and at least one file. §5.2.4's snapshot behaviour is unchanged — the snapshot is taken at registration whichever route reached it — and §5.3.1 gains the control that opens it. **The transition above is the authority on what the screen must satisfy**, and the screen itself is the register's **`B-03`** row, which this reissue applies to Part VII and not to Part V. It carries no `D2-` identifier because it is not an open question: it is specified work that has not been written, and the register is where unapplied rows are tracked.

> **Three rows are added at v0.6, and they close a gap that Parts VIII and IX did not have.** §5.29's two checkpoint outcomes and §5.28.5's correction re-evaluation were specified in v0.5, carried into Part VIII's catalogue and Part IX's traceability, **and never reached Part VII** — which, by §7.2's own rule that *an action not listed for a state does not exist in that state*, meant the console had two controls and a service that formally could not run. **The uphold is the clearest case**: it declines a line, re-runs the chain and moves the ledger, which is the same class of act as *Decline a cost line* — **and that one is listed**. The correction re-evaluation is the `SYSTEM` row, and it is written to name what it may **not** touch as carefully as what it may, because a service that re-evaluates in-flight claims is one edit away from re-deciding them.
>
> **`D2-133` is now two rows owed to Part VII, not one.** §5.5.4's *Hoàn thành kiểm tra tài liệu* still needs an `ASSESSOR`-actor row for `DOC_PROCESSING → UNDER_ASSESSMENT` **and** §5.29's queue implies an `APPROVER`-visible read of a checkpoint from `PENDING_APPROVAL`, which is a read and therefore out of scope here (§7.2's second scoping note) — so the second row owed is the one the register's `B-43` implies rather than that. **Neither is added from inside Part V**, because a part edited from another part stops being the authority on transitions; the three rows above are added *in* Part VII, against D1 v0.5's own rules, which is the distinction `D2-133` exists to keep.

**Five notes the table cannot carry.**

**No transition in this matrix changed when the Policy Data Store was deleted, and that is worth stating rather than leaving to be checked.** The claim state machine, its thirteen states, its transitions, its actors and its preconditions are exactly as they were in v0.1. What changed is which system answers `I-05` at registration and where a payout account is held — neither of which is a state. **The one substantive addition is at §5.2.7**: the adapter can now refuse a structurally invalid benefit tree (V-111 … V-115), which holds the claim in `SUBMITTED` on the operator queue rather than moving it. That is the *absence* of a transition, which is why it is a rule and not a row.

**No transition anywhere has a delivery failure as its trigger.** Part VI F61-R5 states it and the matrix obeys it: a bounced email or an undelivered push changes no state, and `DECLINED → CLOSED` in particular is gated on the approval of the decline, not on the notice arriving.

**`CLM-NOTIF-001` renders `{claimNo}`, and a `DRAFT` has none.** A2 §3.1 triggers it on `SUBMITTED` and Part IV §4.6 fires it on *Gửi hồ sơ*, but the number is not allocated until registration (§5.2.1, Part IV §4.7 F1). Part V §5.2.3 fires it at registration instead. The two are one step apart and the placeholder is not renderable in the earlier one — a wording or trigger question for A2, not a state-machine question. The same applies to `CLM-NOTIF-009` on a withdrawn `DRAFT`.

**A BR-AUTO-4 override leaves the customer with a stale outcome.** They were told *Đã duyệt* by `CLM-NOTIF-005`; the claim then returns to assessment and A2 carries nothing for the reversal. The transition is required and the message gap is real.

**Three transitions exist that a reader scanning the diagram will miss**, and all three are in the table above rather than in a footnote because §7.2's own rule makes an unlisted transition non-existent: `DOC_PROCESSING → APPROVED`, `APPROVED → UNDER_ASSESSMENT` and `PENDING_INFO → PENDING_APPROVAL`.

### 7.3 Four transitions that are not obvious

**A failed cover check does not decline a claim.** It routes to an assessor with the failure named. The reference systems decline automatically here; we do not, because a cover check runs against a snapshot that may itself be wrong — a member registered late, an import that has not run — and a customer who was covered should not be declined by a data gap. D1 §3.2.3.

**A failed payment goes back to the assessor, and the ledger stays final.** The two halves are separately counter-intuitive. It goes to the assessor rather than sitting in `APPROVED` because a rejected transfer usually means the payee data is wrong, and correcting payee data is claim work with a reason attached, not a retry (D1 §4.5, §5.12.4). And the ledger is **not** un-finalised: a reversal is posted (BR-LEDGER-4). Un-finalising is the easier implementation, and it would make the ledger's history unrecoverable and let a concurrent claim see limit that an approved claim has already committed.

**Re-opening a `CLOSED` claim is out of scope** (S-13). There is no transition out of `CLOSED` in MVP 1. A claim that must change after closure is handled as a new claim with a reference to the old one, and the mechanism for that is not built either — Part X carries it as an accepted limitation, not a gap to be filled quietly at build time.

**`CANCELLED` is reachable only before `PENDING_APPROVAL` — the boundary is the lock, not the payment instruction.** A3 §2.1 and D1 §4.6 agree: once a claim has been submitted for approval it can no longer be cancelled, and once anything has been approved it must be **settled or declined**. A claim approved in error is corrected before payment or handled as an overpayment outside the system (S-13). The customer's own withdrawal stops earlier still, at `UNDER_ASSESSMENT` (A3 §1).

### 7.4 The permission principles behind the matrix

Derived from A3, and stated as principles rather than as a second matrix — a summary that contradicts the table two rows above it is worse than no summary. Each row below is true of **every** row of §7.2.

| Actor | The binding constraint |
|---|---|
| `CUST` | Sees only claims they submitted, and never an internal state as itself (A3 §4.3; A2 M-3; Part IV §4.7). After submission they change nothing on the claim except by **adding** documents in response to an information request (F29). Withdrawal is theirs only before `UNDER_ASSESSMENT` |
| **The claimant** | **Not an actor.** A claimant is a **party recorded on a claim** (§3.2.10), not a role, not a login and not a holder of any permission. Where the claimant submitted through the app they are also a `CUST`, and it is `claimant_user_id` — not the claimant record — that §6.2.3's `SELF` scope resolves through. **A claim registered at a counter therefore has a claimant and no app-side reader**, which is correct: nobody submitted it through the app, so nobody can open it there. The distinction matters because a party that acquired a permission by being named on a claim would be a permission nobody granted |
| `ASSESSOR` | Computes and submits; decides nothing that releases money. A3 §2.1 gives a dash on approval (F50), payment (F51) and closure (F52), and **C** on assignment (F43) — they may take and release, never reassign. There is **no permission to apply a deduction ratio** at all (struck row in A3 §2.1, D1 B-09). §4.1 binds per claim on top of this, and §4.12 removes them from any claim they are named on |
| `APPROVER` | Reviews but cannot alter: **R** on F46, F47 and F48. An approver approves, returns, or approves a decline — an approver who disagrees sends the claim back rather than editing it. Everything after the settlement plan is theirs: payment (F51), closure (F52), reassignment (F43), the BR-AUTO-4 override |
| `ADMIN` | **Takes no claim decision and performs no assessment.** They appear in §7.2 on exactly one row — resubmitting a package for extraction (A3 §3.3) — and otherwise read a claim's operational record with clinical detail redacted and the read logged (§4.11). Never approves, pays, closes, cancels or assigns. Their own limits are elsewhere: no self-role change (§4.8), no import commit alone (§4.9), no threshold change alone (§4.7) |
| `SYSTEM` | **The platform never declines.** No row above puts `SYSTEM` in the *Who* column against `DECLINED`, and none ever may — a claim declined because a service was down is indistinguishable from a correct decline (D1 §4.3). The platform does move claims without a person: registration and its four outcomes, the checklist outcome, the two payment callbacks, and closure after a confirmed payment. **But the only *outcome* it may reach alone is `APPROVED`**, through the **four-condition** gate, and every such claim records the conditions it was tested against (BR-AUTO-5) |
| `IDP` | **Never writes to the claim and never changes its state.** `IDP` does not appear in the *Who* column of a single row above: `I-08`, `I-09` and `I-16` are triggers and inputs, and the platform reads them and moves the claim itself. IDP proposes; the Claim Platform decides (D1 §1.4 AR-1, AR-2) |
| `IMO` | **Nothing on a claim, and that is a decision as well as a design.** InsureMO offers claim capability and the client has decided not to use it (C-BUS-09; Framework D-B closes as *none*), so the claim platform is built entirely by us. `IMO` does not appear in the *Who* column of a single row above. What it does hold is the data **every** registration reads — the coverage answer and the benefit tree (§3.3) — so an InsureMO outage stops claims from *starting* while changing nothing about a claim already registered (P-02, §6.4.2). `I-06` is a fire-and-forget registration post whose failure raises an operational alert and blocks nothing (V-505) |

**The `SYSTEM` and `IDP` rows are the architecture.** Everything else in this document is detail; those two are what makes this system different from the one it was compared against.

## Part VIII — Validation catalogue

**Who maintains this part.** **The BA who edits a `V-` rule updates §8.1's range, count and pointer in the same edit, and the BA holding D2 as a whole owns the reconciliation** — the arithmetic at the foot of §8.1's table is checked against the merged file at every reissue, before the reissue is called complete. **This line exists because the counts have drifted once already.** D2 is split-authored by part, every part allocates from its own range, and **an index nobody owns is an index that is nobody's to be wrong** — each editor reasonably assumed the catalogue was somebody else's to reconcile, and the totals fell out of step with the parts while every part was individually correct. **A count is the only thing in this catalogue that can be checked against anything** (§8.1's closing paragraph); an unowned one cannot be checked at all.

### 8.1 How validation identifiers are allocated

Every validation rule has a `V-` identifier, unique across the document, allocated by range so that two parts can be edited at the same time without collision:

| Range reserved | Allocated | Part | Scope, and where the rules are defined |
|---|---|---|---|
| `V-001` … `V-099` | **`V-001` … `V-009` — 9 allocated** | Part II / global | Cross-screen rules that apply everywhere. Defined at **§8.2**, because they belong to no single screen |
| `V-101` … `V-199` | **`V-104` … `V-119` — 16 allocated** | Part III | Policy and member data — the group import (F59), the adapter checks on the benefit tree returned by I-05, **the claimant record (§3.2.10) and the waiting-period anchor (§3.3.3)**. Defined at **§3.8**. **`V-101`, `V-102` and `V-103` are retired** with the administration UI they governed, and are **not reused**; §3.8 says where each survives |
| `V-401` … `V-499` | **`V-401` … `V-408` — 8 allocated** | Part IV | Mobile application. Defined at **§4.11**, **except `V-408`, which is defined at §4.4** beside the figures it governs and indexed at §4.11. **The range is open**: v0.2 reserved it and left it empty, on the grounds that every mobile rule was inline and none was cited twice. The claimant block made that untrue — `V-116` and `V-117` are Part III's rules enforced on a Part IV screen — so the six rules that are cited from more than one place now carry identifiers and the rest stay inline. **`D2-91` narrows rather than closes**: it now asks for the remaining inline rules when D4 is written |
| `V-500` … `V-599` | **`V-501` … `V-599` — 68 allocated. Exhausted** | Part V | Claim web console. Defined inline, at the section where each rule first applies. **`V-500` is the block marker, not a rule** (§5.1, convention V-a) |
| `V-701` … `V-799` | **`V-701` … `V-759` — 59 allocated** | Part V — **overflow** | **Declared in v0.2**, when F58 arrived after the `V-5nn` block was full (§5.20.6), and **extended in v0.3** when the difference register was applied: `V-705` … `V-725`, defined at the section where each first applies. The block is extended rather than a retired number reused, because a reused identifier is how a document starts meaning two things at once. `V-6nn` is Part VI's and is not encroached on. **`V-706` is the twelfth settlement-submission check** and is cited with `V-585 … V-595` (§5.10.2) — it could not continue at `V-596`, which §5.19.4 already holds |
| `V-601` … `V-699` | **`V-601` … `V-632` — 11 allocated** | Part VI | Cross-cutting. Defined at **§6.6**. **`V-630` and `V-631` are new in v0.3**: §6.3.3's action-first audit entry is a nested structure, and a nested structure has invariants a flat row did not have |

**The counts, reconciled.** 9 + 16 + **8** + 68 + **59** + 11 = **171 identifiers defined**, and every `V-` cited anywhere in this document is one of them. The three retired identifiers — `V-101`, `V-102`, `V-103` — are cited only in the sentences that retire them. **`V-099`, `V-199`, `V-499`, `V-699` and `V-799` are range boundaries in this table and are not rules; `V-500` is Part V's block marker (§5.1, convention V-a) and is not a rule either. `V-599` *is* a rule** — §5.19.4's — and the range's upper bound happening to be a live identifier is the one place a reader could miscount this table by one.

**Recomputed from the merged file at v0.5, and the arithmetic moved twice.** It stood at **134** through v0.3. **v0.4 allocated five** — `V-407`, `V-632`, `V-726` … `V-728` — and said so in its §0.6a, **and did not update this table**, which is the exact drift the owner line at the head of this part was written to stop and which it did not stop. **The three stale rows are corrected here rather than re-derived silently**: Part IV 6 → 7, Part V overflow 25 → 28, Part VI 10 → 11, total 134 → **139**. **v0.5 then allocates thirteen** — `V-729` … `V-741` — taking Part V's overflow to 41 and the total to **152**. **The same-day correction of 24 August allocates one more — `V-742`, §5.28.4** — taking the overflow to 42 and the total to **153**, and this table was updated in the same edit rather than a day later, which is the rule the head of this part states and the one v0.4 broke.

**v0.6 allocates eighteen and both counts are recomputed from the merged file before this reissue was called complete.** Seventeen from Part V's overflow — **`V-743` … `V-759`** — and **one from Part IV**, `V-408`, which is the first `V-4nn` this document has allocated for a rule that is not on §4.5's claim form. **Part IV 7 → 8, Part V overflow 42 → 59, total 153 → 171.**

**A count that was wrong for one version is worth more than a count that was never checked**, which is why the correction is written as a correction. **The rule the head of this part states is unchanged and is now stated with a case behind it: the BA who edits a `V-` rule updates this table in the same edit.** v0.4 did not, and the table was wrong for a day.

**Where v0.6's eighteen are defined.** `V-408` at **§4.4** (the counter period on the mobile remaining-limit figures, indexed at §4.11); `V-743`, `V-755` and `V-758` at **§5.28.4**; `V-744` at **§5.28.3a**; `V-745` at **§5.29.2**; `V-746` at **§5.28.7**; `V-747` at **§5.28.5**; `V-748` and `V-749` at **§5.29.3**; `V-750` and `V-751` at **§5.11.4**; `V-752` at **§5.9.1a**; `V-753` at **§5.10.1**; `V-754` at **§5.9.1**; `V-756` at **§5.5.1**; `V-757` at **§5.19.4**; and `V-759` at **§5.28.5**. **Three of the eighteen are the ones a reader should look at first**: `V-743`, because on the pilot register it disables the whole term-decline path; `V-744`, because it is the only thing standing between an expression builder and a text box; and `V-750`, because it closes a control that was firing into an empty room.

**Where v0.5's fourteen are defined.** `V-729` at **§5.9.1a**; `V-730` and `V-731` at **§5.9.3**; `V-732` at **§5.10.2** (the thirteenth submission check); `V-733` at **§5.11.4** (the gate's third condition); `V-734` … `V-737` at **§5.28.3** and **§5.28.4**; `V-738` and `V-739` at **§5.28.5**; `V-740` and `V-741` at **§5.29.3**; and **`V-742` at §5.28.4**, allocated by the same-day correction — a class `J` or `E` term may never carry a decline effect, which is the one-directional half of a constraint §5.28.3 F11 had stated in two directions. **`V-723` is extended rather than reallocated** — the counter key gains `periodKey` and `counterType` and the identifier does not move, because the rule is the same rule with a longer key (§5.9.3).

**One correspondence across parts, stated so that neither side looks like a duplicate.** **`V-117`** (§3.8) is the rule that a claimant declaring themselves the insured must carry the insured's name and identity number. It is enforced on the app at §4.5 F13 and F14, and on the console at **`V-709`** (§5.20.5), which is Part V's own identifier for the same requirement on its own surface. **They are one rule with two enforcement points, not two rules** — the pattern §2.2 anticipates when a *Validation* cell names an identifier from another part. `V-116` and `V-118` have no console identifier because §5.4.2 F37 and §5.5.1 carry them inline.

**Where the six rules added to Parts III, IV and VI in v0.3 are defined.** `V-116`, `V-117`, `V-118`, `V-119` at §3.8; `V-401` … `V-406` at §4.11; `V-630`, `V-631` at §6.6. **And v0.4's five**: `V-407` at §4.11, `V-632` at §6.6, `V-726` … `V-728` at §5.4.5.

**Where the twenty-one rules added to Part V in v0.3 are defined.** `V-705`, `V-715` at §5.6; `V-706` at §5.10.2; `V-707`, `V-708` at §5.7.2; `V-709`, `V-710` at §5.20.5; `V-711`, `V-712` at §5.3.2; `V-713` at §5.3.3; `V-714` at §5.4.1; `V-716`, `V-717`, `V-725` at §5.10; `V-718`, `V-719` at §5.22; `V-720` at §5.14.1; `V-721` and its three lettered clauses at §5.23.3; `V-722` at §5.11.4; `V-723` at §5.9.3; `V-724` at §5.5.2.

**Each rule is defined once, in the section where it first applies**, with its condition, the A2 message it raises and whether it is enforced on the client, the server or both. This part is the index, not a second copy — a rule stated twice is a rule that will disagree with itself.

**The allocated count is part of the entry, and it is there to be reconciled.** A range on its own says only which numbers a part may use; it cannot be checked against anything. A count can: every identifier cited anywhere in this document must fall inside its part's range **and** have a definition, and the two totals must agree. Without the count, a part could cite fifteen identifiers and define none of them, and nothing in this catalogue would say so — which is exactly what had happened before this revision.

### 8.2 The global rules

These are the only ones defined here, because they belong to no single screen.

| # | Rule | Where enforced | On failure |
|---|---|---|---|
| **V-001** | **Every mutating action is authorised server-side**, against A3, on the claim's current state and the actor's scope — regardless of what the client sent | Server | `403`, and an audit entry with outcome `DENIED` |
| **V-002** | **Every money value is an integer number of dong.** A payload or form carrying a decimal is rejected, not rounded | Client and server | Field-level, `CLM-VAL-*` per screen |
| **V-003** | **Every percentage is integer basis points** in storage and on the wire (D3 §1.2). `20%` is `2000` | Server | Contract-level `422` |
| **V-004** | **Every date is interpreted in Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh.** A date with no offset is not assumed UTC | Server | `422` |
| **V-005** | **No claim-affecting write succeeds on a claim in `PENDING_APPROVAL`, `APPROVED`, `PAID`, `CLOSED`, `DECLINED` or `CANCELLED`** except the transitions Part VII lists | Server | `409`, message per screen |
| **V-006** | **Optimistic concurrency on the limit ledger.** A calculation submitted against a stale counter version is rejected and re-run against current counters, never merged | Server | `409`; `D2-67` |
| **V-007** | **Idempotency on every inbound webhook and every outbound instruction.** A repeated `I-08` or `I-12` delivery changes nothing; a repeated `I-11` does not pay twice | Server | Silently idempotent, logged once |
| **V-008** | **A message shown to a person is always a complete A2 template**, never assembled from fragments (§2.6, A2 M-8) | Build-time check plus server | Template validation failure — ***(new A2 item needed — **D2-88**)*** (§6.1.4, §6.5.1, V-604), *whose allocation is **D2-88***. **Corrected in v0.3**: this cell cited `D2-84`, which is the session and re-authentication policy item (§6.5.3) and has nothing to do with a template |
| **V-009** | **A system failure is never rendered as a claim outcome** (A2 M-6, D3 G-3). Operational states map to the customer-facing status in Part IV §4.7 — *Đang xử lý chứng từ* for `DOC_PROCESSING` and `EXTRACTION_ERROR` alike — never to a status of their own | Client and server | — |

### 8.3 A gap worth naming, and how much of it is left

**Most of Part IV's mobile rules are still stated inline rather than carrying `V-4nn` identifiers.** Almost all of them are single-field checks with an A2 code beside them, and inline is legible where a catalogue reference would not be. But it means those rules cannot be cited from D4's acceptance criteria the way the console's can.

**Eight of them are no longer in that position** — six in v0.3, `V-407` in v0.4 and **`V-408` in v0.6**, the last of which is a rule enforced on **two mobile screens and cited from the console's `V-730` and `V-731`**, which is the same argument one step further out. §4.11 allocates `V-401` … `V-406` to the rules v0.3 made citable from more than one place — the loss-type set, the date chain, the accident narrative, the claimant's email, the other-documents group and the customer-sent date — because **a rule enforced on two surfaces and named on neither is exactly what the identifier scheme exists to prevent.** The claimant block forced the question: `V-116` and `V-117` are Part III's rules running on a Part IV screen, and there was no way to say so without a Part IV identifier to cite them from.

**What is left is a real cost, and it is deferred rather than denied.** The remaining inline rules should get identifiers when D4 is written, at which point each acceptance criterion has something to point at. **`D2-91` narrows** to that remainder.

#### 9.1a What Part III requires of InsureMO

Part III specifies no feature we build except F59. What it does specify is **the read model two of InsureMO's features must satisfy**, and this table is how a reviewer checks that nothing the claim engine depends on was lost when the store was deleted.

| **F07** — benefit schedule query as at a date, returned as a tree | The tree two to three levels deep with a parent pointer and a `depth`; annual, per-event and per-day caps; **count limits with `0` = unlimited**; **`INHERIT` co-payment**; the deduction ratio with its condition; **waiting periods across the six condition classes with `null` meaning *cannot arise***; effective dating; the whole tree in one response | §3.2.3, §3.2.4, §3.3.4, §3.4 | R-IMO-02, R-IMO-11 **Confirmed — the decisive item**; C-IMO-01, C-IMO-01b **Confirmed** |
| **Both** | Effective-dating behaviour beneath the as-at-a-date query | §3.2.3, §3.3.4, §3.4 Case D and E | **C-IMO-05 — capability confirmed, contract detail open.** The one where a surprise costs design rather than a mock |

**Every row above is a requirement on a third party with no fallback behind it** (§3.1, Framework RK-14), and the only mitigation is to evaluate the sandbox against A5 v1.2 benefit by benefit — **C-IMO-06**. §3.4 Cases A to E are written to be run as exactly that test.

### 9.2 The rules that shape more than one screen

Most business rules touch one section and are cited there. **These fifteen** are load-bearing across the document, and a change to any of them is a change to several screens at once — so they are listed with everywhere they land.

| Rule | What it fixes | Screens it shapes |
|---|---|---|
| **D1 §1.4 AR-1** — IDP proposes, the platform decides | Every IDP-sourced value is editable and attributed | §5.6, §5.7, §5.8 |
| **D1 §1.4 AR-4** — every assessor action is on the claim | No second system, no synchronisation; the deep link is read-only | §5.6, §5.14 |
| **D1 §4.2** — the policy snapshot | Nothing on a registered claim is re-read. **The load-bearing rule of v0.2**: it is now the only local record of what the contract said (§3.7 point 1) | §3.7, §5.2, §5.4, §5.9 |
| **D1 §5.3** — the fourteen-step chain with a stated base per percentage | The calculation is displayed step by step, not as a total | §5.9, and §5.8 on re-run |
| **D1 §5.6 / B-09** — the deduction ratio is a policy term | No assessor input, no grant, no ceiling. Its answer comes from F57 | §5.7, §5.9, §5.17 |
| **D1 §5.8 / B-12** — the **four**-condition gate | Confidence is not a condition; a cut claim never auto-approves; an open term checkpoint holds the claim back **whichever class raised it** (D-5); **and from v0.6 an outstanding duplicate signal does too** (`V-750`), which is what makes `BR-DUP-2`'s warning reach anybody on the population that settles unreviewed. **Evaluated once, in `DOC_PROCESSING`, and never re-entered** | §5.6, **§5.9.1a**, §5.11, §5.15, **§5.29**, Part VII §7.2, and §6.3's log |
| **D1 v0.5 `BR-TERM-10`** — a term whose `clauseRef` is provisional may not decline | **On the pilot register this is every term**, so step 4's auto-decline branch cannot fire at all: `V-743` marks the term unciteable, §5.29.5's uphold control is absent, and the blocker is `D2-159` | **§5.28.3 F3**, **§5.28.4**, **§5.29.3**, **§5.29.5**, §5.9.4, Part VII §7.2 |
| **D1 v0.5 `BR-TERM-9`** — a term may test only facts available at the step its scope runs at | Enforced **when the term is saved**, not when it is evaluated, against **A1 §4.11's *available from step* column** — which is why §5.28.3a's builder filters the fact list by scope rather than refusing on save | **§5.28.3a**, `V-744`, §5.28.3 F9 |

| **D1 BR-LEDGER-1** — provisional at calculation, **final at approval** | Approval moves the ledger; payment does not | §5.9, §5.11, §5.12, §5.13, Part VII §7.1 |

| **A2 M-6 / D3 G-3** — a failure is never an outcome | Three operational states are hidden behind *Đang xử lý* | §4.7, §5.3, §6.1, Part VII §7.1 |
| **D1 §5.3.1 BR-TERM-1** — evaluate all, not first-match | Every term in scope is evaluated and **every result is recorded whether it fired or not**; every `clauseRef` that fired is carried into the decline, not only the first | **§5.9.1a**, **§5.9.7**, §5.10.1's letter preview, §5.11.1 row 4, §6.3's log |
| **D1 §5.3.1** — class J and class E may **never** auto-decline, and **`BR-TERM-7`** — a class `J` or `E` term may never carry a decline **effect**, while a class `D` term may carry any effect including `CHECKPOINT` | The engine raises a checkpoint with the clause quoted and a person decides. It is what **§5.29** exists for, what constrains `predicate` at **§5.28.3**, and what `V-742` refuses at the register | **§5.28**, **§5.28.1a**, **§5.29**, §5.9.1a, §5.11.4 |

**A5 is the one that looks safest and is not.** B-01 confirmed its *structure* and left its *figures* to be replaced from a real product. Replacing figures changes §4.3, §4.4 and §5.9's worked example and nothing else. **Replacing the structure would change the data model in §3.2** — which is why A5 §0.1 lists the seven mechanisms any substitute must still exercise. **And from v0.2 it would do more than that: it would invalidate the demonstration.** C-IMO-01 was closed as *demonstrated* against A5 v1.2 specifically. A structural change to A5 is a change to the thing InsureMO confirmed it could carry, and it re-opens **RK-14** rather than merely editing three sections.
